#3071. Walmart Has Raised Its Dividend 53 Straight Years. Why I'd Buy It Before December and Never Sell.

Walmart's 53-year dividend streak points to a durable business. Advertising, memberships, and global growth could keep it expanding for decades.

Some stocks stand out because they've proven they can reward shareholders for decades, and Walmart (WMT -0.23%) is one of those stocks, having raised its dividend for 53 consecutive years. Looking ahead, with new growth opportunities emerging across advertising and e-commerce, here's why investors might consider buying this retail giant before the new year and holding it forever.

The latest increase brought the company's annual dividend to $0.99 per share, up from $0.94 in the previous fiscal year, just as it's done for the past 53 years.

But Walmart's dividend history is about more than returning cash to shareholders. It's proof of something more important: the durability of its business, as Walmart is built around supplying necessities at competitive prices, regardless of whether the economy is booming or slowing.

On top of that, its enormous scale, established customer relationships, and extensive distribution network make it difficult for competitors to replicate what it has built. Instead of relying on its traditional retail business, Walmart has spent years expanding into faster-growing areas that could support decades of future growth.

Retail has traditionally been a relatively low-margin business. Walmart moves enormous volumes of products, but selling groceries and household essentials leaves limited room for profit growth. That's why growing advertising and membership businesses have become increasingly important.

From there, it's important to consider Walmart Connect, the company's advertising platform. Since Walmart has direct relationships with millions of shoppers and access to valuable shopping data, it can offer brands opportunities to reach consumers much closer to the point of purchase.

In fact, that strategy is already driving growth.

Walmart's global advertising business grew 38% in the second quarter of fiscal 2027, while its U.S. advertising business grew 43%, excluding VIZIO. Plus, the acquisition of VIZIO gives Walmart an opportunity to expand its advertising reach into connected television, creating another channel where it can monetize customer relationships.

Meanwhile, memberships offer another opportunity. For example, Walmart+ and Sam's Club memberships encourage repeat purchases while creating recurring fee revenue.

Plus, they give customers more reasons to consolidate their shopping with Walmart rather than spending across several retailers. With that, global membership fee revenue rose 17% in the second quarter of fiscal 2027.

Meanwhile, beyond advertising and memberships, Walmart is expanding globally to drive the next phase of its growth.

These days, Walmart's growth isn't limited to the U.S. In fact, the company operates across multiple international markets, including Mexico, Canada, China, India, and several countries in Central America and Africa. These businesses provide exposure to different markets and give Walmart more opportunities to expand.

On top of that, its international strategy opens up opportunities in digital markets. In India, for instance, Walmart has a significant stake in Flipkart, one of the country's major e-commerce platforms. As India's digital economy and consumer markets expand, it offers a long-term opportunity that's difficult to replicate through traditional U.S. retail operations.

Likewise, Sam's Club is another important part of this opportunity, as its membership-based warehouse model generates recurring revenue and encourages customer loyalty and repeat spending. In particular, the format is seeing significant potential in markets such as China and Mexico, where membership growth and digital adoption can support expansion.

Still, investors should weigh that growth potential against the stock's valuation and risks.

The vast majority of Wall Street analysts covering the stock rate it a buy or strong buy, with an average price target of $131.45. These days, the stock trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of about 38, so many investors are already expecting meaningful growth. Still, Walmart's strong competitive position and growth opportunities help justify that premium.

That said, owning Walmart isn't without risks. For one, its enormous size makes growth challenging, while competition from other retailers could pressure margins and market share. Despite that, Walmart's staying power comes from sticking to the business model that has sustained it for decades, while finding new ways to grow and adapt.

Ultimately, Walmart has spent 53 consecutive years proving it can continue to reward shareholders. Looking ahead, with e-commerce, advertising, and memberships creating new opportunities, its growth runway is far from over. And that's why investors might consider buying shares before the new year and holding them for life.

For all that, it helps to look beyond short-term noise and focus on stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Top Wall Street analysts' recommendations can help investors gain clarity, as these experts conduct in-depth research to pick stocks with attractive growth prospects.

Enterprise software and cloud infrastructure company Oracle (ORCL) recently announced better-than-expected results for the first quarter of fiscal 2027. The quarter benefited from solid growth in cloud infrastructure revenue.

After hosting a series of investor meetings with Ken Bond, Oracle head of investor relations following Q1 earnings, Guggenheim analyst John DiFucci reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $400. Oracle remains a Guggenheim Best Idea, he said.

"We continue to believe ORCL is a decade stock, driven by the massive (and profitable) opportunity ahead for AI training and inferencing," said DiFucci. He also cited the traditional Public Cloud business and additional AI-enabled cloud database and cloud applications for his bullish stance. DiFucci expects all the factors to drive revenue and profit acceleration over the next few years.

While Oracle delivered 850 MW of data center capacity in Q1 FY27, Bond cautioned that Infrastructure as a Service revenue in any quarter depends more on the timing of when that capacity comes online, than on the headline MW number. DiFucci expects IaaS growth to stay strong, with full-year growth expected above Q1 FY27's 120% constant currency rate. Management expects total revenue growth to accelerate sequentially throughout fiscal 2027, as the faster-growing infrastructure business makes up a larger share of the mix.

DiFucci addressed concerns regarding customer concentration, saying OpenAI's share of total remaining performance obligations has dropped from 80% last June to about 50% now, and is expected to keep falling as new contracts are signed with new and existing customers.

"RKLB has assembled launch, spacecraft, components, payloads and optical communications, with Neutron and Iridium completing medium-lift and applications/spectrum in 2027," said Gesuale.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that with the completion of the Iridium acquisition, Rocket Lab will become the only vertically integrated space company with positive free cash flow (FCF). The deal will add a deployed constellation valued at more than $3 billion, globally coordinated L-band spectrum and about $500 million in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) and $300 million in free cash flow (FCF).

Gesuale highlighted RKLB's strong revenue and backlog growth and progress toward positive EBITDA and FCF in 2027/2028. Rocket Lab is moving from a heavy investment phase into monetization, with estimated revenue growth of 59% in 2026, the analyst said, noting that RKLB's backlog has more than doubled to almost $2.4 billion from $1.1 billion in Q3 2025.

Given strong growth projections, the analyst expects RKLB's gross margins to expand from about a 35% trough in 2027 to about 47% by 2030, while R&D spending is estimated to decline from ~35% of sales in 2026 to about 10% in 2028, creating substantial operating leverage as the platform matures.

Gesuale ranks No. 369 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of about 17%. See Rocket Lab Statistics on TipRanks.

J.P. Morgan analyst Doug Anmuth recently upgraded Meta Platforms (META) to buy from hold and raised his price target to $820 from $640. Despite the year-to-date underperformance of META, the 5-star analyst still sees significant upside, as Meta is in the early stages of launching frontier models and AI-powered offerings beyond advertising, particularly the Muse AI agent and Meta Model API access.

"Frontier models are at the core of Meta's product and monetization pipeline over a multi-year period, and its path toward superintelligence," said Anmuth.

In the summer of 2025, Meta set a goal to rebuild its Meta Superintelligence Labs team and deliver frontier AI models within a year, the analyst said. The team appears to have met its goal, rapidly advancing from the rollout of Muse Spark 1.1 in July to Muse Spark 1.3, which is competitive with Claude and GPT models, Anmuth said.

Meanwhile, Meta's Watermelon product will expand opportunities in consumer products, business intelligence, and Family of Apps engagement, the analyst said. The product will enhance internal operations and overall efficiency, said Anmuth, who's confident of Meta's ability to bring consumer-driven AI products to its extensive user base of 4 billion and views its distribution network as a competitive advantage.

While Meta has focused on frontier models and AI product development, Anmuth also sees solid opportunity in its AI infrastructure capacity, which he believes will support future compute needs.

#3069. The Moat Isn't The Agentic Data; It's Knowing What The Data Means

Siddhartha Rao is a VP & Distinguished Engineer at Oracle. He has been working on AI and machine learning for the last decade.

Nearly every serious conversation about enterprise AI now includes the same four words: “Context is the moat.” Then everyone nods.

But ask what context actually is, and the room goes quiet. That silence is expensive. Companies are funding agents to “chat with their data” without being able to say what those agents need to know.

I lead generative AI services for Oracle’s AI Data Platform, so I’m not a neutral observer. Still, I’ve watched enough pilots stall to have opinions about why. Here are six of those opinions:

The fashionable answer to the question of context is data gravity. Bring the models to where the data already lives.

Fine. Do it. But a model sitting next to a petabyte it doesn’t understand is like a tourist outside of a library in a language they can’t read.

The advantage belongs to whomever understands the data (like which of three revenue tables finance actually trusts) and knows which instrument fits which question, whether that means forecasting for demand, Bayesian estimates for risk or deterministic rules for eligibility.

The language model’s job, working out what the data means, is narrower than the hype suggests.

Context includes metadata, the workflows a business actually runs, an ontology of the concepts it reasons in, and an understanding of how its structured and unstructured data relate.

Context is not raw rows stuffed into a prompt. Size is not meaning, and we should stop pretending otherwise.

The piece most teams miss is the tool description. An agent never reads your data model. It reads the descriptions of the tools it’s allowed to call. A generic “run SQL” tool tells it nothing. A tool described in the business’s own language, scoped to what that agent should see, tells it how to think.

Prompt engineering was about how you ask. Context engineering is about what the model is told the world contains.

Should context live in one platform or stay spread across lakehouses, databases and applications? It’s a false choice. No CIO wants yet another copy of everything, with permissions that drift from the source. Leave the data where it lives and query it in place.

What has to consolidate is meaning; one semantic layer that bounds the model, orchestrates its tools and decides what each user may touch. That layer, not storage, is the control point.

Gartner predicted in June 2025 that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, citing costs, unclear value and inadequate risk controls. But read that list again. Nowhere does it say the model wasn’t smart enough.

Pilots run on curated data for a few users who can see everything. Production runs on thousands of users with row-level, column-level and role-based permissions. Agents make it harder by creating data the access model never anticipated, such as summaries, memories or knowledge graphs.

If an agent tells one user what it learned from another’s query, then all you’ve done is build a very polite data leak.

Will better reasoning models make proprietary context obsolete? No. The frontier has moved from capability to cost. A model that rediscovers your schema on every question burns tokens, takes a different path each time and returns an answer nobody can trace. That’s a brilliant new hire with amnesia, billing by the hour.

Context is amortized reasoning. You pay once to understand the business, and every later question inherits it. That math changes only when inference is nearly free, reproducible and able to audit itself back to source rows. I wouldn’t bet the roadmap on all three.

When an agent acts on stale or over-permissioned context, who owns the failure? Juvenal asked the governance question nearly 2,000 years ago: Who watches the watchmen? If you can’t reconstruct what the agent saw, how old it was and whose permissions applied, the answer is the CIO.

So, build governance in. Citations should trace to the business concept the agent thought it was answering and to the exact rows it used. Memory should point back to source data with a freshness timestamp. A stale finding presented as current is the most dangerous kind of wrong, because it’s plausibly right.

If you fund one thing on Monday morning, make it the expertise, in-house or through a partner, to build an ontology, semantic models and progressive disclosure. Give the model the map first, then reveal detail only as each question demands. It’s cheaper, more accurate and easier to govern because every disclosure becomes a checkpoint for permissions, freshness and lineage.

Before you sign with any vendor, put these six problems on the table. Their answers will tell you more than their demos.

#3068. Eaton vs. Vertiv: Which Industrials Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Eaton and Vertiv both ride the electrification wave, but their growth profiles and valuations diverge sharply heading into 2027.

As the energy transition and data center demand accelerate, choosing the right infrastructure play is vital. Should you bet on Eaton Corp. (ETN +0.39%) or Vertiv Holdings Inc. (VRT +1.33%) for your portfolio?

Eaton is a global giant managing power across diverse industrial sectors, while Vertiv specializes in cooling and power systems for the booming data center market. Both companies benefit from massive electrification trends, but they offer different levels of diversification and growth potential for investors looking to capitalize on modern infrastructure needs.

Eaton operates as a massive power management company, serving markets ranging from utilities and data centers to aerospace and mobility. In its latest annual report, filed for FY 2025, the company noted that six major customers account for approximately 22% of revenue in its Electrical sectors. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, particularly as the firm seeks to expand its reach in specialized industrial segments.

In FY 2025, revenue reached about $27.4 billion, which represented growth of approximately 10.3% over the prior year. The company reported a net margin of close to 14.9%, resulting in net income of roughly $4.1 billion. This growth reflects strong demand for electrical infrastructure as global power needs continue to rise.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.6x. This ratio shows that total debt is equivalent to 60% of shareholder equity, indicating a moderate level of borrowing. The current ratio, which compares short-term assets to short-term liabilities, was roughly 1.3x, while free cash flow reached about $3.6 billion after subtracting capital expenditures from operating cash.

Vertiv specializes in providing the cooling and power infrastructure required to keep data centers and communication networks running. The company serves prominent hyperscale and cloud providers including Microsoft Corp. (MSFT -1.65%) and Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN +0.39%). It also maintains a strategic partnership with Infineon Technologies (IFNNF +0.35%) to supply power semiconductors for high-performance computing.

In FY 2025, revenue reached approximately $10.2 billion, reflecting significant growth of about 27.7% compared to the previous year. Vertiv reported net income of around $1.3 billion, which corresponds to a net margin of roughly 13%. This rapid expansion highlights the company's leading role in providing critical digital infrastructure within the industrial stocks sector.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 0.8x. This metric indicates that the company carries $0.80 in debt for every dollar of shareholder equity. The current ratio stood at approximately 1.5x, and free cash flow for the period reached about $1.9 billion, representing the cash left over after the business pays for its necessary capital projects.

Eaton faces operational integration risks because it frequently uses strategic acquisitions to expand its business. The company is also exposed to global supply chain disruptions and inflationary pressures that could impact the cost of raw materials and labor. Furthermore, cybersecurity threats and potential challenges from spinning off its Mobility business segment could affect its operations.

Vertiv carries risks related to its heavy reliance on the growth of data centers and overall spending on artificial intelligence. The company competes against large global manufacturers like Schneider Electric (SBGSF -0.38%) and Legrand (LGRVF -4.42%) for market share in power and cooling solutions. Additionally, the long-term, fixed-price nature of many contracts means that any errors in estimating costs could reduce its future profitability.

Eaton looks cheaper with a lower Forward P/E using future earnings estimates and a lower P/S ratio based on sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Eaton is a blue chip industrial company that is benefiting from megatrends, including energy transition, electrification, digitalization, and infrastructure spending. The company has been experiencing strong orders and record backlogs, which has led investors to believe top-line sales and profits should steadily increase. In particular, data centers have been a high-growth area for Eaton, with orders up more than threefold in 2026 and an order backlog that extends out 12 years. Management also anticipates strong growth in the aerospace and utility end markets.

In its third quarter, reported in early November, Eaton saw sales rise 28% to $8.9 billion, with net income up about 30% to $1.34 billion. Eaton is expected to finish 2026 with sales up more than 20% over 2025 and improved net income. For 2027, Wall Street analysts expect sales and net income to rise about 12%.

Vertiv has been a specialist in computer cooling systems since World War Two, and it also offers complementary products for mission-critical technological infrastructure, such as uninterruptible power supplies. The AI-driven data center boom presents a long-term opportunity for Vertiv, especially for its liquid cooling systems. Liquid cooling is better for quickly removing heat from high-powered chipsets. Vertiv believes one-third of the total addressable market for data center cooling will eventually use liquid solutions (technically, some air-cooling and heat-dissipation systems will always be needed to work in tandem with liquid systems).

For 2026, Vertiv revenue should rise 44% to $14.7 billion, with net income shooting up about 90% to $2.5 billion as AI data center demand powers the business. Those figures are much stronger than anticipated just a few months ago. For 2027, analyst consensus has Vertiv revenue jumping about a third, with net income up more than 40% to $4.6 billion.

These are both traditional industrial businesses that have tapped into the trends of electrification and AI, and are posting exceptional growth as a result. Which is the better buy? It may be a toss-up, so Eaton's slightly cheaper P/E and P/S ratios win the day.

#3066. Visa and American Express Both Raised Their Dividends 16% This Year, but Only 1 of the Stocks Is Up in 2026

Not all payment card giants are created equal.

Was it coincidence or a keeping-up-with-the-Joneses strategy?

Last month, payment card giant Visa (V -0.92%) announced a 16% dividend raise. That came less than eight months after longtime rival American Express (AXP -0.25%) declared its own 16% hike. And those increases followed a nearly 15% dividend raise trumpeted by their veteran peer Mastercard as 2025 came to a close. Despite the matching 16% bumps, the stock prices of Visa and Amex have traveled in strikingly different directions this year.

To put it briefly, Visa stock is up, and Amex is down; the former has risen by nearly 22% year to date, well higher than the S&P 500 index's 8% gain, while Amex has fallen by almost 14%. For the curious, Mastercard is also in index-beating territory, with a nearly 16% increase. Here's how that looks on a handy graph:

One big factor in that divergence is recent quarterly performance. Both Visa and Amex routinely post very healthy growth rates on both the top and bottom lines. After all, paying for basically anything by card -- from snacks to utility bills to large pieces of furniture -- is the rule rather than the exception for consumers these days. Marry that with a still-thriving economy (despite some pull-back due to rising prices), and you've got a fine source of organic growth for payment card companies.

With this, investors expect Visa, Amex, and Mastercard to not only perform well, but to outperform. For the most part, all three deliver... well, at least they did, until Amex's last two reported quarters. In both its second and third frames, it missed -- if only barely -- the consensus analyst estimate for revenue. Technically, the company underperformed, which was a psychological blow to investors.

Amex also struggled to contain expenses; one reason its competitive moat is high is the many perks it offers cardholders through its vaunted Amex Rewards program. These aren't free for the company to provide, plus in our current age where consumers often value experiences over material items, uptake of those goodies has been brisk lately. In the second quarter, total expenses grew by 12% year over year, outpacing the 10% rise in revenue. The subsequent quarter was a wash, with both increasing by 9%. Investors are far more comfortable when revenue growth eclipses spending.

With Visa, Amex, or Mastercard, it's important to be aware of the difference between an open-loop and closed-loop operator. Visa and Mastercard are the former; this means they act only as facilitators of transactions made on the cards bearing their logos. They extend none of the credit; instead, this is done (typically) by banks or other financial institutions.

Closed-loop operators, exemplified by Amex, span the entire credit card ecosystem. They are both the transaction facilitator and the issuer, so when you swipe with an Amex, the company is also lending you the money.

There are pluses and minuses with each model. Very briefly, I'll sum up my favorite advantages: Open-loopers are asset-light, collecting a tiny percentage of every transaction from their massive volume -- after all, who doesn't have at least one Visa or Mastercard these days? Closed-loop operators, unlike their rivals, don't have to split transaction fees with intermediaries such as issuers. Also, they earn revenue from card fees and the interest charged to folks who don't pay their balances on time.

Two other developments are negatively impacting Amex, as a closed-looper, and benefiting the two others. One is the federal government's long-simmering Credit Card Competition Act (CCCA), which would require large banks to use more than one payment network to process credit card transactions. This means no more exclusivity for Visa or Mastercard, which is currently common industry practice. Closed-loop companies would be exempt from this requirement, to the obvious advantage of Amex.

The fact that this act has essentially gone nowhere in Congress -- despite President Donald Trump promising more than once he'd sign it into law if it's passed -- is a drag on Amex stock and a boon for Visa and Mastercard.

The second of the two developments is the Federal Reserve's interest rate hike in September and, given the persistence of inflation, the possibility that more raises are on the way. Again, Amex acts as an issuer, so it's interest rate sensitive. Yes, it'll earn more revenue from cardholders carrying over balances, but those people could rein in their spending as their APRs rise.

While I believe Visa fully deserves that index-topping rise in its share price, I don't feel Amex is being treated fairly with the decline in its equity.

The latter company -- a longtime favorite of beloved master investor Warren Buffett, by the way -- boasts an enviable set of advantages. Despite having many ambitious competitors, its plastic is still considered to be the most prestigious by many consumers, who are willing to fork over the often high annual "membership fee" for the privilege of holding it. Meanwhile, the average Amex cardholder is relatively affluent and likes using their Centurion or Platinum card to buy things. It's telling that even through lean economies, Amex has usually managed to post healthy top- and bottom-line growth.

On top of that, its dividend yield beats Visa's, at 1.1% versus 0.7%, and its forward P/E is far lower (less than 16 against 28).

I've been bullish on both companies for quite some time, but with Amex's recent downward trajectory, I'd be more inclined to buy that stock than I would Visa.

#3065. The Crypto Fear & Greed Index Is in "Extreme Fear" Territory. History Says This Happens Next.

Periods of fearfulness like this one are rarely reversed quickly, but conditions still improve eventually.

The Crypto Fear & Greed Index, a high-level measure of market sentiment, is, as of Nov. 16, at an "extreme fear" reading of 13, marking a reversal from the widespread bullish mood this summer that saw the index at 80 on Aug. 25. Bitcoin (BTC +0.90%) traded at $78,565 on Aug. 25, versus $64,931 on Nov. 16.

Wild volatility and extremes of sentiment have been common for Bitcoin. Here's what history suggests will happen next, given the fearful market.

In an analysis in February 2026, Coin Bureau co-founder Nic Puckrin found that when crypto's Fear & Greed Index fell or lingered below 25, Bitcoin's average 90-day returns afterward were just 2.4%. For example, when the index was at 24 on Jan. 21 of this year, Bitcoin's price was $89,364, and it has fallen 26% since then.

Part of the reason this dynamic exists is that extreme market fear usually occurs during crypto bear markets or immediately after crashes or hacks that destroy investor confidence. But even if the 90-day returns aren't that great on average, waiting longer -- perhaps even a lot longer -- tends to give way to a recovery eventually.

In the coronavirus crash of March 2020, the index sank to 3. Despite plunging along with everything else during that period, Bitcoin is now up nearly 1,190% since then. Buying during that panic took confidence in the asset, but it paid off.

Nearly two-thirds of 2021's 100 largest altcoins — esentially all cryptos aside from Bitcoin — were down by more than 90% as of Oct. 21 of this year, and nearly all coins outside the top 100 effectively lost all their value. That means it is not wise to simply buy a basket of declining cryptocurrencies and hope that time will heal all wounds afterward. Focusing on assets that were growing strongly during the current slump is a better approach.

Neither of those coins needs its price to go up for its fundamental value to increase. And while Bitcoin hasn't done well, it's still getting scarcer over time, regardless of what its price is doing. Each of its halving events cuts by 50% the reward miners receive for each block added to the chains, occurring roughly every four years, and slowing the supply growth rate.

There's no rush to buy anything right now. Don't let the market's fearfulness become yours, and stay focused on the long term in the meantime.

#3063. Is Nvidia Stock's Trading at 10x Forward Earnings the Bargain of the Century or Dead Money Hiding in Plain Sight?

Nvidia trades at a valuation similar to that of companies with far less impressive growth.

If you weren't sure how valuable Jensen Huang was to Nvidia (NVDA -1.29%), then simply look at the stock over the past month. Nvidia's stock has fallen nearly 30% in the past month (as of the morning of Nov. 16). Huang admitted marital infidelity in a letter to the company on Nov. 8, and his resignation was announced Nov. 12.

This is an enormous move for a stock with a market cap of nearly $3.9 trillion, even after the decline. Huang co-founded Nvidia 33 years ago, and the company now reportedly controls 90% of the general-purpose graphics processing unit (GPU) market, which powers the technology many believe will completely transform the world as we know it.

Nvidia stock currently trades at roughly 10 times its projected fiscal year 2028 earnings (fiscal 2028 ends in January 2029). Is the stock the bargain of the century or dead money hiding in plain sight?

Whatever you think about Huang, who resigned after extramarital affairs came to light, including with one woman who may have been a Chinese spy, there's no denying that Huang was a strong CEO.

He built Nvidia into the juggernaut it is today and has become the voice for the entire AI industry. That said, no person is bigger than a company like Nvidia. Even without Huang, Nvidia still has a dominant product and the team that made it what it is today.

A big reason I think the stock is struggling is that Huang's ouster is not simply about an extramarital affair. It's also about national security, the quality of Nvidia's chip sales, and their end location.

Specifically, Huang's relationship with Alice Huang (no relation) — the controlling shareholder of a Singaporean data center company called MegaSpeed — has raised concerns that Jensen Huang may have been compromised and that Nvidia chips may have entered China illegally.

Former President Joe Biden's administration had only allowed Nvidia to sell older-generation chips to Chinese companies, due to national security concerns. In April 2025, the Trump administration told Nvidia it would need to obtain export licenses to sell chips to China. Since then, Nvidia has said there have been virtually no chip sales to China.

While many details remain unknown, reporting by media outlets, including The Information, has found that a network developed by Alice Huang allegedly helped funnel billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia chips to Chinese companies.

This will raise many questions for investors, and activist short-seller Culper Research estimated in May that a fifth of Nvidia's fiscal year 2026 sales may have illegally ended up in China. (Short-sellers make money when a stock they hold falls in value.)

If this proves true and the Trump administration or Congress can impose even tougher export restrictions, could Nvidia's revenue and earnings be revised downward? Or will it need to spend more for better compliance?

There could also be government investigations that lead to regulatory fines or other punitive measures.

Don't get me wrong, Nvidia stock at 10x fiscal 2028 projected earnings looks incredibly attractive. In Nvidia's fiscal 2027 second quarter, the company grew revenue by 106%; grew earnings by 128%; and posted a 75% gross margin. Companies that do that often see their stocks trade at earnings multiples that are multiples higher.

But one of the big questions at Nvidia is whether the company has been over-earning and whether all of these circular financing agreements it engages in reflect its true financial health.

Unfortunately, none of these questions have an easy answer and will require significant research that may be beyond the reach of the typical retail investor.

On the bullish side, there is still a very good chance Nvidia will continue to perform well and remain the dominant chip player. For all these reasons, I think investors can begin nibbling on Nvidia stock. But I don't think it's time to go all in just yet.

More information about all of this will certainly emerge in the coming weeks and months. Whether it's good or bad for the stock remains the big question mark.

#3061. The Chief Architect As The Enterprise Orchestra Conductor

Robert Sheesley is an award-winning executive, speaker and author, known for technology-enabled transformation and new value creation.

An orchestra can assemble extraordinary musicians and still deliver an uneven performance. Every section may play its own part beautifully, yet the composition suffers when timing, interpretation and balance fail to come together.

Enterprises face the same challenge. Talented people, strong business units and substantial technology investments do not automatically produce strong enterprise results. Departments pursue reasonable objectives, projects meet their delivery milestones and new technologies arrive with compelling promises. Customers and employees experience how those contributions fit together.

The chief architect helps shape that collective performance. Working across organizational boundaries, the architect connects strategic intent to the capabilities, investments and operating changes required to deliver it. AI extends this responsibility by introducing new ways to understand the enterprise and new participants in its work.

The conductor metaphor is useful because it places architecture where it belongs: close to the relationship, between strategy and execution.

A conductor understands the full score, listens across sections and helps specialists contribute to a shared interpretation. The chief architect brings a comparable perspective to the enterprise, helping leaders see how their decisions affect the whole.

Business leaders retain accountability for results. Executives determine strategic priorities and authorize investments. The architect contributes the enterprise design, evidence and coordination needed to make those choices workable.

A strategic ambition such as improving customer loyalty or increasing operational efficiency leaves considerable room for interpretation. Different business units can pursue the same ambition through incompatible investments.

The chief architect helps make the intended outcome explicit. What must customers experience differently? Which business capabilities must improve? What changes in information, processes, technology and employee skills would make that improvement possible?

Kaplan and Norton’s work on strategy maps provides a useful foundation. It connects organizational capabilities and internal processes with customer and financial outcomes. Those connections express management’s reasoning about how investment should create value. They also give the enterprise assumptions it can test through execution.

For example, a company seeking greater customer loyalty might propose faster service resolution. Achieving that outcome could require better diagnostic knowledge, reliable access to customer history, clearer authority for resolving exceptions and additional employee training.

Architecture makes these relationships visible before the enterprise commits to a solution.

Business capabilities describe what the enterprise must be able to do, such as manage suppliers, fulfill orders, develop products or resolve customer issues. They provide a useful basis for discussion across departments because they remain recognizable even as reporting structures and systems change.

The chief architect uses that perspective to connect strategy with investment. Leaders can examine the capabilities their objectives depend on, assess current performance and identify gaps that deserve attention.​

A strategy becomes consequential when leaders allocate capital, talent and management attention.

The technology investment board adds an essential dimension to the conductor metaphor. It provides a forum for evaluating investments across the enterprise, balancing priorities, risk and forecasted return, and provides for mechanisms to properly evaluate and adjust the portfolio as conditions change.

The chief architect brings the architectural evidence into that conversation: capability gaps, shared dependencies, reuse opportunities, accumulated debt and the consequences of sequencing decisions. Portfolio management contributes delivery and resource information. Finance helps assess affordability and benefits. Business sponsors explain the operational changes required to realize value.

Together, these perspectives support decisions about what to fund, defer, reshape or stop.

A balanced portfolio must sustain current operations while improving performance and developing future capabilities. Required security or compliance work may have limited discretionary choice. Foundational investments may enable several later initiatives without producing an immediate standalone return.

Architecture helps make those relationships explicit. A shared data capability, for example, may support customer service, planning and multiple AI applications. Evaluating it only within one project could understate its contribution. Counting its full benefits in every dependent project could overstate the portfolio’s return.

The architect helps leaders understand the common foundation and allocate costs and benefits consistently.

Timing matters just as much as selection. Several individually attractive projects can overwhelm the same subject matter experts, compete for integration capacity or require employees to absorb too much change at once. A credible portfolio accounts for the enterprise’s ability to perform the work.

AI contributes to this operating model in two ways.

First, it can strengthen architectural work. With appropriate access and validation, AI can help examine documentation, identify possible dependencies, compare designs and summarize evidence for investment reviews. These capabilities can reduce the effort required to investigate a complex enterprise.

The resulting analysis still needs scrutiny. Missing information can produce incomplete maps. Recommendations can overlook operational constraints. Forecasts depend on the quality of their data and assumptions.

The chief architect establishes how that evidence will be checked and how much confidence a decision should place in it.

Second, AI becomes part of business execution. Assistants help employees interpret information. Models support forecasts. Agents can perform defined actions within workflows.

Leaders must decide who owns the outcome, what authority AI receives and how people detect and address failure. Adding AI to a fragmented process can increase the speed at which fragmentation produces consequences.

Ultimately, the chief architect earns the conductor’s role by helping the enterprise turn strategic intent into a coordinated, measurable performance. Business architecture identifies the capabilities that matter; investment governance directs resources toward them; process management connects those capabilities through the daily work that delivers customer value.

AI can strengthen this performance by informing decisions, supporting people and executing appropriate tasks within clearly defined boundaries. Its contribution depends on sound process design, accountable business ownership and feedback that guides continuous improvement.

The chief architect keeps these relationships in view, helping leaders judge success through better customer outcomes, stronger operational performance and the enterprise’s growing ability to adapt and learn.

#3058. GM Just Switched Stock Exchanges. Here’s Why That Matters for Investors

The automaker’s move to the Nasdaq could put its stock in front of hundreds of billions of dollars in index funds.

General Motors (NASDAQ: GM) first listed its stock on the New York Stock Exchange in 1911. Apart from a break after its 2009 bankruptcy, it traded there for more than a century.

As of today, Nov. 17, it trades on the Nasdaq. The ticker is still "GM," and shareholders don't need to do anything. From a stock trading or stock ownership perspective, nothing is really changing. But the switch could matter more than it seems, because it puts GM in line to join one of the most widely tracked indexes in the world.

The Nasdaq-100 is composed of the 100 largest nonfinancial companies listed on the Nasdaq, and only on the Nasdaq. That's why GM could never be in it before. Funds that track the index, including the popular Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ -0.39%), hold more than $600 billion combined and must buy every stock in the index.

GM says the move reflects its "technology-driven strategy," and that may be true. The company has emerged as one of the clear leaders in EVs, and its software and services business is growing rapidly. But it's hard to ignore the timing. Nasdaq ranks eligible companies by market value on the last trading day of November, and the annual changes are typically announced in mid-December. GM's switch comes two weeks before this year's cutoff.

Walmart (WMT -0.23%) made the same move last year, but it switched on Dec. 9, after the November cutoff. It missed the December changes and had to wait until January to join the index, a change that analysts estimated would bring about $19 billion in buying from index funds. There are new rules in place since Walmart joined the index; it's now a quarterly review process, but the timing of the switch matters.

GM is much smaller than Walmart, with a market cap of about $72 billion. That's still big enough to rank in the top 100. Alnylam Pharmaceuticals was the largest eligible company outside the index heading into last year's reconstitution, with a market cap of about $60 billion, and it was added. Of course, nothing is official until Nasdaq announces the changes.

If General Motors is added to the Nasdaq-100, index funds will have to buy its shares, which often gives a stock a short-term boost. But to be perfectly clear, that's a one-time event and is likely to be a short-term catalyst for the stock at best. It doesn't make GM's vehicles sell better or change its profits. Over time, GM's stock will still depend on what it always has: its earnings, its electric-vehicle and software plans, and how much stock it buys back.

In short, this is a good reminder that where a stock trades can decide which funds have to own it. I wouldn't buy GM for a potential index bump, but if you already like the business, it's a potential tailwind worth keeping an eye on.

Personal finance writers and editors share their favorite ways to be resourceful.

Have you ever thrown away groceries that spoiled before you got around to using them? Or bought a new jacket despite already having half a dozen in your closet?

It’s easy to let things go to waste and accumulate more than we need.

Use Less Stuff Day, which lands on Nov. 19 this year, encourages us to rethink our consumption habits and make more mindful, environmentally friendly choices.

That might mean squeezing every last drop out of what you’ve got, finding creative ways to reuse things or simply buying less.

I keep a couple of simple tricks up my sleeve to extend the life of my family’s clothing: OxiClean soaks and basic sewing skills. You’d be surprised by how many things you can salvage with a little cleaning and mending.

I asked my fellow Nerds to share some of the ways they reduce waste and unnecessary spending. Maybe you’ll pick up an idea or two.

Pamela de la Fuente, managing editor: My husband grew up with a “make what’s in the house” kinda family. I didn’t. But this weekend while looking for spaghetti I found some crispy rice cereal, and I knew we had marshmallows from a bonfire a few weeks ago so I said, “I’m going to make crispy rice treats with this for the kids and get rid of this cereal.” (Surprisingly, it was not stale.) I still had cereal left, so I added it to some chocolate protein bars I love to make and my son said, “These are 9 out of 10. Usually they are 7 out of 10!”

Karen Gaudette Brewer, head of content: I’m a big “make big batches of food and freeze it” person, so I can drive everyone nuts reminding them that we really do have food at home. That freezer also holds grated lemon zest and cubes of those last little bits of chicken broth and wine so that I can easily make pan sauces and not waste that last half cup of goodness.

Jessica Cano, content coordinator: I save the tops from strawberries after cutting them for my kids. We use some to make strawberry balsamic vinegar, some to make strawberry syrup and the rest go in the freezer to be used for smoothies. Keeps me from having to buy frozen fruit and multiple vinegars.

Pantry shopping can result in less food in the trash and fewer trips to the grocery store. It can also make experimenting with new recipes a little more exciting. Take a page from Managing Editor Athena Cocoves, who says, “Sometimes we pretend we're on ‘Chopped.’”

Ryan Brady, lead writer: Rotating toys with our kids has helped them get more enjoyment out of the same toys versus constantly buying new toys. We put a bunch of toys they're bored with in a bin, and months later, take one out and bam — it's like a new toy all over again!

Kim Lowe, head of content: I invested a whole $12 in a lint remover last winter that transformed all my old sweaters into almost new!

Laura McMullen, editor: Almost all of my kids’ clothes are thrifted or hand-me-downs. My friend group of parents has kids from age 2 to 7, all of whom are about six months apart. We’ve developed a hearty clothing exchange. It’s fun to see my friends' kids wear hand-me-downs that we got from my brother’s family almost 10 years ago.

Look for other ways to salvage your belongings or get them secondhand. That might include watching a vacuum repair tutorial on YouTube, borrowing books from the library or purchasing used tools from Facebook Marketplace. The goal: Keep more stuff in circulation and out of landfills.

Abby Doyle, lead writer: Composting isn’t as fussy as it seems. Once you get into it, you start seeing would-be waste as stuff to feed your new backyard buddy. Junk mail, paper bags, slimy spring mix … it’s all food for my “pet dirt.” And my garden has legit never looked better.

Yuliya Goldshteyn, editor: Instead of throwing away kid art, I reuse it as wrapping paper throughout the year. Bespoke gift wrapping for everyone! I haven’t bought gift wrap for five years now.

Caitlin Constantine, editor: I repurpose glass jars and plastic containers. It always seemed like such a pity to throw perfectly good containers into the recycling after one use, so now I reuse them before I recycle them.

Before you toss something, ask yourself, “Is there another way I can use this?” An old T-shirt makes a good cleaning rag, for example.

Being resourceful often means getting as much mileage as possible out of what you have.

#3055. The Hidden Costs Of DIY AI: Why The Real Expense Begins After The Prototype

Sundar Balasubramanian is Senior Vice President of Product Management at Icertis.

​Artificial intelligence (AI) has created the false impression that enterprise software has become remarkably inexpensive to build. In many ways, that perception is justified. Business teams can now create applications, agents, workflows and copilots in a matter of days or weeks instead of months. Capabilities that once required large development teams and technical expertise are now accessible through natural language prompts and off-the-shelf AI services.

What many organizations often underestimate is that the prototype is the easiest part of the journey. The real challenge begins when AI applications become business-critical and require ongoing governance, support, security, maintenance, model management and operational accountability over time.

As companies rush to build AI-powered solutions, they are discovering that while the economics of creating software have changed dramatically, the economics of operating enterprise software have not. Reliability, accountability, governance, support and continuous improvement remain essential requirements. The difference is that organizations often encounter these realities later in the process, after the excitement of rapid deployment has taken hold.

One of the most exciting aspects of AI is the speed at which teams can transform an idea into a working application. This capability has unlocked a new wave of experimentation across the enterprise. Departments that previously relied on centralized development resources can now create solutions tailored to their own needs, accelerating innovation and expanding access to technology.

But leaders should be careful not to confuse a successful pilot with a scalable enterprise solution. An application serving a small group of users within a single department operates in a relatively controlled environment. The requirements change significantly when that same solution is expected to support thousands of employees across multiple business units, regions and regulatory environments. At that point, reliability becomes a critical business requirement.

This is where many organizations encounter an unexpected reality: Scaling an AI solution introduces more complexity than building it in the first place. What begins as a low-cost experiment can become a long-term operational commitment, requiring sustained investment in maintenance, support and continuous improvement as the business evolves.​

Organizations not only have to maintain the technology itself, but also ensure the expertise required to keep it effective. AI models, technologies and business requirements continue to evolve. Therefore, keeping pace requires ongoing investment in specialized skills, research and development, and product improvement long after the initial AI tool is deployed. This is one reason many organizations rely on specialized software providers rather than building everything themselves. They gain access to teams whose primary responsibility is staying ahead of technological change, benefitting from expertise and best practices developed across a broader customer ecosystem. Perhaps most importantly, they establish long-term accountability for support, product evolution and continuity.

Contract lifecycle management is a timely example of where the economics of building and operating often diverge. AI can accelerate the creation of contract review tools, clause extraction workflows or conversational interfaces. What is less visible is the ongoing investment required to support a system that manages sensitive commercial data, integrates with enterprise systems and provides the business context needed for AI to deliver reliable, actionable outcomes. These costs extend far beyond maintenance alone and appear in places organizations least expect.

AI has introduced a fundamentally different cost structure than traditional enterprise software. Consumption, utilization and optimization matter now more than ever before as the economics of how AI is deployed become just as important as what it can do. Specialized software is engineered to address business requirements at enterprise scale, while minimizing token spend.

Generalized AI applications, in comparison, can turn what appears to be a modest operating cost into a substantial recurring expense as usage grows because they are not purpose-built for the complex, high-volume processes of an enterprise.

AI consumption has already become a boardroom discussion, shaping budgeting, governance and long-term planning in much the same way that cloud computing did. Many organizations initially focused on the flexibility and speed cloud platforms provided, only to discover later that ongoing consumption required deliberate oversight to keep costs aligned with business outcomes. As adoption scales, organizations need to consider not just where AI is being used, but how to apply it most efficiently for the needs of their business.

Many organizations approach governance as something that must be addressed before deployment. Policies are established. Reviews are conducted. Controls are defined. Once those steps are complete, there can be a tendency to assume the governance challenge has been solved.

In reality, governance often becomes more important after deployment than before it. Once employees begin relying on AI to support decisions and workflows, new questions inevitably arise. Who owns the application? Who approves modifications to prompts or underlying models? How should outputs be monitored and evaluated? What metrics should be used to measure performance and business value?

These are not questions that can be answered once and forgotten. They require continuous attention. Governance evolves from a compliance-oriented exercise into an operational discipline focused on ensuring that controls remain effective as technology, regulations and business requirements continue to change.

Governance also carries direct cost implications. Without clear ownership and oversight, organizations can encounter duplicated solutions, inconsistent outputs, excessive model usage and unexpected expenses associated with resolving issues related to accuracy, security or compliance. What initially appears to be a faster path to innovation can ultimately create inefficiencies that erode the value the initiative was intended to deliver.

Organizations that underestimate this responsibility may find themselves devoting far more time and resources to managing governance than they anticipated when building the original solution.

The broader lesson, however, is that AI has changed the cost of building software, but it has not eliminated the responsibilities that come with operating enterprise technology. The most successful organizations look beyond the speed of development and evaluate AI through a total cost of ownership lens. The prototype may be inexpensive. The real investment begins when the solution becomes part of how the business runs.

#3054. Should You Buy Micron Stock Before Dec. 9?

Micron is allowed to begin buying back stock on Dec. 9.

During the early phases of the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution, developers raced to procure as many graphics processing units (GPUs) as possible. As the hyperscalers move forward with data center build-outs, AI infrastructure budgets are flowing downstream into adjacent chip solutions – namely, high bandwidth memory (HBM) and dynamic random-access memory (DRAM).

These secular tailwinds are helping Micron Technology (MU -2.51%) generate record revenue, earnings, and cash flow. Nevertheless, investors have recently experienced a sharp reversal, with Micron stock declining roughly 30% since the company reported fiscal fourth-quarter earnings on Sept. 30.

Although uncertainty surrounding AI infrastructure spending has weighed on semiconductor stocks recently, Micron has an important catalyst coming up. Beginning Dec. 9, the memory manufacturer will have more flexibility to repurchase its stock following restrictions associated with its federal CHIPS Act funding agreements.

During Micron's fiscal 2026 (ended Sept. 3), the company repurchased just 2.5 million shares for $650 million. That followed fiscal 2025, when Micron didn't repurchase any shares.

The limited activity is partly attributable to restrictions associated with Micron's CHIPS Act funding agreements. During the first two years of the five-year agreement period, stock repurchases were generally restricted to specified amounts intended to offset dilution from employee stock compensation, unless otherwise permitted by the Department of Commerce.

During Micron's fiscal third quarter earnings call in June, CFO Mark Murphy explained the company's long-term capital allocation strategy, stating, "Over time, we expect to return 100% of our excess cash to shareholders."

Murphy indicated that Micron intends to increase shareholder distributions around Dec. 9, with share repurchases expected to be the primary mechanism. On Oct. 8, Micron's board of directors expanded the company's existing share repurchase authorization to $35.16 billion.

When companies buy back their own stock, they reduce the number of shares outstanding. Even if net income remained unchanged, a lower share count translates into higher earnings per share (EPS), which can support stock price appreciation if investors maintain the same valuation multiple.

Consider a hypothetical $10 billion repurchase: At Micron's Sept. 30 share price of about $1,065, the company could purchase roughly 9.4 million shares. At its price as of this writing (Nov. 16), the same $10 billion would purchase approximately 13.6 million shares. In other words, Micron's plummeting stock price allows the company to retire nearly 45% more stock with the same outlay.

This example illustrates why buying back stock at depressed valuations can create more value for shareholders than repurchasing them at elevated prices. If Micron's earnings remain strong while its outstanding share count declines, EPS could accelerate faster than net income. That combination is attractive and could reignite enthusiasm around the long-term outlook for AI infrastructure spending.

To me, Micron's expanded buyback program gives investors a new reason to consider buying the stock before Dec. 9. The company's recent decline could allow management to retire substantially more stock than would have been possible at Micron's elevated prices just a couple of months ago.

For investors with a long-term time horizon who can stomach some short-term volatility in the semiconductor industry, buying Micron stock before the repurchase program becomes available could prove more rewarding than waiting for the buybacks to begin.

#3053. Lame-Duck Congress Faced With Averting Another Shutdown

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Legislators must act quickly if they want to avoid a shutdown that would land in the midst of the holiday season.

With the midterm election in the rearview and a new Democrat-controlled Congress about to be sworn in Jan. 4, the current class of legislators finds itself working to avoid an impending government shutdown that would start after Dec. 11.

Over the summer, the House of Representatives passed a stopgap bill that would extend government funding at its current level through the December deadline, in a bid to push the funding battle until after midterm elections. The government had been set to run out of money after Sept. 30.

Disagreements over spending priorities could once again leave the government facing a shutdown. Lawmakers face a deadline, with little time to negotiate a longer-term spending deal before the extension expires on Dec. 11. The lame-duck session — the period between the November elections and the start of the new Congress — gives outgoing lawmakers one final opportunity to reach a long-term agreement or extend the deadline into 2027.

Some Senate Democrats are threatening to withhold support for a deal unless it includes restrictions on funding President Donald Trump’s war with Iran. Meanwhile, Trump is urging Senate leaders to use budget reconciliation to fund an additional $350 billion in supplemental defense spending.

However, leaders in both parties are publicly supporting a short-term stopgap that would keep the government funded until after the current lame-duck session ends.

Every year, Congress is supposed to pass 12 spending bills to keep the government’s lights on. These appropriations bills fund those programs already approved by Congress, including defense, the IRS, food assistance, veterans’ benefits and national parks.

The deadline to fund programs for the next fiscal year is always Oct. 1. Without passing appropriations bills or approving a stopgap that kicks the deadline down the road, the government shuts down.

In the past few funding cycles, Congress has relied on multiple short-term continuing resolutions to keep the government temporarily running.

In 2025, the government shut down for the longest period in U.S. history (Oct. 1 to Nov. 12, 43 days) while this year was marked by the longest partial shutdown ever (Feb. 14 to April 30, 76 days). Why didn’t Congress pass the funding bills in 2025? The two parties were deadlocked over Democrats’ ultimately unsuccessful efforts to permanently extend expiring Obamacare subsidies and roll back recent Medicaid cuts in the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA).

A second shutdown — this one partial — began on Feb. 14. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) shut down after lawmakers failed to reach a deal to reform Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) tactics. DHS funding became a flashpoint following the fatal shootings of Renée Good on Jan. 7 by an ICE agent and Alex Pretti on Jan. 24 by a CBP agent, both in Minneapolis. The DHS shutdown followed a four-day partial shutdown that ended Feb. 3.

On April 30, the House passed a bill approved by the Senate to fund most of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The deal fully funded all DHS offices with the exceptions of ICE and Border Patrol. Democrats supported the deal, despite it lacking any of the restrictions on the two agencies that they had been demanding throughout the shutdown.

» MORE: How to prepare for the next government shutdown

At 43 days, the 2025 government shutdown was the longest in history. There have been 22 shutdowns since 1976 and most are short-lived — a few hours or days, at the most.

Before then, there hadn’t been a shutdown since 2018-2019. That shutdown, which lasted 35 days, arose in a dispute over funding for Trump’s border wall in his first term.

Before that there was a 16-day shutdown in 2013, as negotiations over the Affordable Care Act dragged on. In 1995 and 1996, two shutdowns totaled 26 days.

Federal workers bear the brunt of impact from government shutdowns.

During a shutdown, there are ripple effects on delivery of government services and programs.

National parks may close or operate without services.

Federal student aid application processing could be delayed.

Food and drug inspections will be delayed.

The IRS can’t verify income and Social Security numbers, which could cause delays for some mortgages and other loan approvals, as well as tax refunds.

Flights will still operate, but there could be delays if TSA agents and air traffic controllers, who are considered essential employees, decide to call out of work, leading to staff shortages. Even small shortages can have a big impact: During a 2019 government shutdown, the absence of just 10 air traffic controllers at two airports grounded flights and caused delays for the Eastern Seaboard. (Read more on how the shutdown affects travel.)

Social Security and Medicare will keep going, but some administrative functions may be suspended, and telehealth appointments may be interrupted.

Unemployment benefits will continue — states administer compensation — but there could be application processing delays if the shutdown lasts long enough.

Food benefits through Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and the accompanying WIC program will continue — both run on contingency funds. WIC funding will only last one month, and SNAP could be strained after 30 days, as well.

The postal service — the USPS is not funded by the federal government.

Federal student loan payments — accounts are serviced by private companies.

Public schools will remain open — they’re funded by state and local governments.

Amtrak will continue operations — it is operated by a for-profit company.

See more details on how a government shutdown could impact you. The shutdown has had trickle-down economic effects. One immediate and direct impact during the previous shutdown was a suspension of federal economic data. Most of that data wasn’t released during the shutdown. That’s a problem because the government’s official data releases guide the markets, the Federal Reserve and business decisions.ent’s official data releases guide the markets, the Federal Reserve and business decisions.

(Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images News via Getty Images)

#3052. ETF Launch Boom, Closure Bust: How to Spot a Fund That Might Not Last

Every ETF has to start somewhere, but not every ETF sticks around.

Nearly $1.8 trillion in net inflows into U.S.-listed exchange-traded funds (ETFs) this year highlights how popular these funds are. What's not to like? ETFs offer diversification, low costs, and easy trading. They're simple to buy and sell like stocks, while providing access to broad markets, sectors, or investment strategies.

The reality is this, though: Despite ETFs' growing popularity, a new ticker doesn't guarantee a long life. U.S. funds launched 1,023 ETFs through August 2026, a record pace and 52% ahead of the same point in 2025. Yet launching a new fund is easier than attracting enough investors to keep it running.

It takes more than a good idea to sustain an ETF. Here's what to look for if you want an ETF with staying power.

A media-savvy CEO, a clever theme, or a memorable ticker, may attract early interest, but without substance, they don't guarantee long-term success. What matters is whether assets and fund flows grow over several months or whether the ETF remains small, even after it's had enough time to attract an audience.

If a fund doesn't seem to grow, ask yourself whether anything sets it apart from larger, more established alternatives. Does it offer anything that those other funds don't offer?

While a small asset base isn't proof a fund will close, persistently low assets can make it harder for the fund to cover operating costs and earn a healthy return.

According to FactSet, as of March 31, 2026, 38.4% of U.S. ETFs had less than $50 million in assets. Again, that's not necessarily a bad sign, especially for a newly launched fund. However, given the effort it takes to attract investors, a fund that struggles to gain traction may not last long.

Low trading volume and a wide bid-ask spread can make buying or selling more costly. Review an ETF's spread and whether its market price is above or below its net asset value. While these measures can't predict whether a fund will close, they do reveal how costly or difficult it may be to trade.

The now-defunct U.S. Defiance Next Gen H2 ETF (HDRO) illustrates how difficult it can be for small thematic ETFs to attract investors and remain afloat.

When it was launched on March 9, 2021, HDRO looked good. It was a thematic stock ETF focused on companies involved in the hydrogen economy, including hydrogen production, fuel cells, and related equipment and infrastructure.

However, by April 2025, the fund announced it was liquidating. While Defiance didn't state a specific reason for the fund's closing, its poor performance likely tells the story. By the time the announcement came, HDRO's assets had dropped from about $65.9 million to $13.88 million.

While it's true that HDRO briefly gained traction, that early interest didn't last, and the fund's value and assets shrank.

The best strategy is to treat a new ETF as a product to evaluate, not as a promise that a fund will be around forever. Look at its assets, age, flows, trading costs, and strategy, and then review them periodically. It's the least you can do for a well-balanced portfolio.

#3051. The Next Great Infrastructure Reset

Rajjie Sarmey is Founder and Chief Visionary Officer of FutureProof CXO, advancing governed AI, enterprise strategy and durable value.

The next great enterprise infrastructure reset may not begin inside a data center. It could begin beneath an ocean, at an electrical substation, along a telecommunications corridor or within an orbital network. Its consequences could cascade all four domains.

For decades, enterprise technology strategy centered around computing capacity, consolidation, connectivity, virtualization and cloud migration. We optimized utilization, negotiated consumption economics, reduced technical debt and pursued geographic scale and redundancy. Those disciplines remain essential today but are now insufficient.

As we navigate the remainder of 2026 and prepare for 2030, the strategic question shifts from where enterprises compute most efficiently to where they can operate securely, safely, reliably, lawfully and economically when interconnected infrastructure assumptions fail.

I define this emerging discipline as Infrastructure-Consequence Economics—a fundamental shift in how boards, CXOs, investors and architects evaluate digital infrastructure.

Three documented indicators reveal this transition.

1. Electricity is becoming a strategic computing constraint. The International Energy Agency’s 2025 “Energy and AI” report projected global data center electricity consumption rising from approximately 415 TWh in 2024 to 945 TWh by 2030 under its base-case scenario, acknowledging significant uncertainty in the future.​

2. Infrastructure is entering an extraordinary capital cycle. McKinsey estimated in April 2025 that data centers would require approximately $6.7 trillion in cumulative worldwide capital by 2030, encompassing AI and conventional computing workloads.​

3. Digital globalization depends on concentrated physical connectivity. A 2025 International Telecommunication Union report highlighted that submarine cables carried more than 99% of international data flows.​

These projections aren’t guarantees, but they signal increasing interdependencies. Converging capital intensity, energy availability, physical connectivity and geopolitical risk are now reshaping enterprise computing economics.

Submarine cables connect geographies, financial markets, cloud environments and global commerce. A multiregional cloud architecture may still depend on shared cable corridors, telecom providers and/or landing stations. Geographic separation doesn’t guarantee dependency independence.

AI demands dependable electricity, transmission capacity, cooling, water where applicable, network connectivity, physical security and suitable locations. Available compute without sufficient power delivery isn’t deployable capacity.

As we race toward 2030, infrastructure readiness and energy availability may influence workload placement as significantly as processor performance or cloud pricing.

Aviation communications, wireless networks and airborne platforms extend operations beyond terrestrial infrastructure. Across aviation, distributed industries, logistics and emergency response aspects, resilience demands managing spectrum, coverage, backhaul and continuity risks.

Mission-critical connectivity depends on coordinated terrestrial, airborne and satellite capabilities and not isolated networks or assumed independence.

Satellite communications and positioning, combined with navigation and timing services, strengthen operational continuity when terrestrial systems fail but introduce distinct risks that involves interference, cybersecurity, terminal dependencies, service concentration and regulatory constraints. Resilience architecture must extend into the physical and jurisdictional systems supporting them.

Decades of leading transformations across mission-critical regulated environments reinforces one principle: Redundancy isn’t resilience when independent systems share common failure points. Multiple cloud providers, facilities and backup ecosystems may share critical dependencies across identity, security, power, telecom and operations.

Resilience is measured not by provider count but by the ability to sustain or restore critical business services within defined risk and recovery tolerances. It mandates mapped dependencies, independent recovery paths, tested failovers, well-defined decision authority and verifiable recoverability. In high-risk environments, resilience must be demonstrated, not merely documented.

Traditionally, infrastructure economics focus on acquisition costs, capacity, consumption, utilization and operating efficiency. These measures remain necessary but rarely capture the full economic impact of infrastructure failure, prolonged disruption, geographic concentration or sovereign restrictions.

I propose evaluating infrastructure decisions through five interconnected dimensions:

1. Economic Sustainability: Full life cycle costs across capital, compute, energy, networking, cooling and operations.

2. Dependency Resilience: Exposure to correlated failures across facilities, providers, utilities and networks.

3. Jurisdictional Assurance: Data residency, contractual enforceability, regulatory obligations and operational control.

4. Recoverability: Demonstrated restoration capabilities, RTOs and RPOs, and service continuity.

5. Trusted Business Outcomes: Measurable value within defined security, reliability, safety and risk tolerances.

The governing principle is to optimize not for the lowest infrastructure unit price but for risk-adjusted cost per trusted business outcomes. Every material infrastructure investment should be evaluated against its life cycle economics, correlated failure risks, tested recoverability, jurisdictional obligations and measurable business consequences.

For boards, the question is whether executive leadership understands the infrastructure dependencies, capital exposures and failure scenarios that could compromise enterprise investments. For CXOs, architecture must connect business criticality, recovery engineering, workload positioning, cybersecurity and economic accountability.

For investors, infrastructure valuations demand scrutiny beyond announced compute capacity, meaning power availability, utilization, customer commitments, financing costs and monetization assumptions. For founders, the strategic optionality can outweigh capital-intensive infrastructure ownership.

Ownership doesn’t equal control. Multicloud doesn’t equal resilience. Sovereignty doesn’t equal security. Capability doesn’t equal returns. Competitive advantage requires mastering these distinctions.

By 2030, which enterprises will outperform?

1. Enterprises owning the most infrastructure?

2. Enterprises purchasing compute at the lowest price?

3. Enterprises architecting the freedom to operate across changing technological, economic and geopolitical situations?

My conviction favors the third scenario, provided freedom is measurable, tested and economically sustainable.

The next phase of infrastructure reset isn’t simply about where intelligence runs. It’s about whether enterprises retain their authority, resilience and economic capacity to act decisively when the operating conditions change.

Infrastructure will increasingly determine whether enterprise strategy creates sustainable business value. Will competitive advantage come from infrastructure ownership and lowest cost compute, or will it come from proven resilience, risk-adjusted enterprise economics and strategic freedom?​
