#3050. Hit by the FAA Ground Stop? How to Get Your Money Back

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site or when you click to or take an action on their website. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

If your travel plans were disrupted, here's how you can get refunded or rebooked.

An estimated 1.5 million travelers had their flight plans upended on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, after the Federal Aviation Administration announced a rare nationwide ground stop. That number comes from the flight data firm Cirium, which tracked passengers scheduled to depart U.S. airports that day after the stop was declared. The ground stop lasted more than four hours.

That ground stop lifted at 8:15 p.m. ET on Friday, but the ripple effects could be massive. Planes are out of position for the weekend, and some travelers are still trying to reach their destinations or get refunds on flights and other expenses.

NerdWallet travel writer Craig Joseph was among those affected. He was flying out of Asheville, North Carolina, for a one-night trip to a college football game, and learned his flight was delayed by three hours. Because it was a quick trip, and he had booked with frequent flyer miles that could be redeposited into his account, he canceled. Moments later, his flight — and every other one on the departures board — was canceled.

He canceled his hotel before the deadline, too, so his only sunk cost was the football ticket. But not all travelers will be so lucky.

If your travel plans were impacted, here's how you can get your money back.

Don’t count on calling customer service. Major airlines have been overwhelmed with customers asking for help.

As of Friday night, Southwest’s automated phone number said it would take several hours to get a callback from a human. American Airlines’ automated line said it would take at least two hours to reach a human. Frontier Airlines wouldn’t even let us speak to a human, and instead sent us to a chatbot.

Skip the chatbots and long waits. Instead, do this:

Check the airline’s app or website, and look for any emails or other alerts. Most airlines are proactively notifying affected passengers with rebooking options, and you may be automatically rebooked.

Get a refund or rebook online or through the airline's app. Every major airline has issued a travel waiver due to the ground stop, which gives you more flexibility to rebook without a change fee, often without charging for fare differences. More on that below.

Check your travel insurance. Because the ground stop was outside the airlines' control, they may not offer vouchers for hotels or food. If you paid these costs out of pocket, you might be able to get reimbursed from your travel insurance policy, if you purchased one, or your card's coverage. More on that below, too.

Under U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) rules, you are entitled to a full refund if your flight is canceled or significantly delayed — no matter the reason — and you decide not to travel and turn down other forms of compensation like travel credits. The money must be delivered to your original payment method, even if you bought nonrefundable tickets.

If your flight disruption meets the DOT criteria, make sure you're getting a full refund. Some airline waivers offer a travel credit as a default option. Credits typically expire, and you won't get value from them until you redeem them. With a refund, you can get your money back within days.

If you booked with points or miles, you'll generally get those redeposited to your loyalty account, plus a refund of any taxes and fees you paid.

But if you still want to forge on with your travels, most airlines are allowing affected passengers to rebook new flights without owing a change fee or fare difference, which is more generous than usual. If your original travel dates were Nov. 13 or 14, and you purchased your tickets on or before Nov. 12 or 13, you're likely eligible for these flexible change policies.

Depending on the airline, you might have even more flexibility. For example, Southwest’s more generous rebooking policy applies to flights scheduled through Monday, Nov. 16.

Just note that each airline has its own limitations on when you must take that new flight, so check with your airline to ensure you book within the allowed window. Here are the waiver pages for major airlines:

Right now, you and everyone else who was supposed to be on that Friday afternoon flight are vying for limited seats on aircraft flying the same route over the next few days. Get creative if the flight you need is booked up. Think about whether a nearby airport might be possible. You might also opt for a train or rental car.

If your flight disruption also cost you a hotel night, a rental car, a concert or sports ticket, or some other prepaid piece of your trip, here's your best chance at getting that money back, too:

Call the hotel or rental property directly. Although not guaranteed, your host may waive a cancellation penalty or no-show fee for a documented flight disruption like this one. Have your canceled or delayed flight confirmation handy, and ask kindly.

For nonrefundable event tickets like concerts or sports games, you’re unlikely to get a direct refund. Check the specific event's refund policy first (and it never hurts to ask!), but your best bet in most cases is reselling the ticket through a platform like StubHub, SeatGeek or Vivid Seats rather than counting on a refund from the original seller.

Keep every receipt and email confirmation. Whether you're asking a hotel for an exception or filing an insurance claim, having your original flight confirmation, the cancellation or delay notice and your other prepaid reservations documented in one place will make every one of these conversations faster.

If you have a standalone travel insurance policy: Travel delay and missed connection benefits may cover you for a disruption like this one, according to the insurance marketplace Squaremouth. If you already hold a policy, contact your provider's 24-hour emergency assistance line directly rather than waiting to file a claim after the fact.

If you don't think you bought travel insurance, check your card terms. Many premium travel credit cards include travel insurance for covered events as a card benefit, assuming you paid for the trip with your card. But in this case, trip cancellation and interruption coverage likely wouldn't apply, because covered events are limited to things like illness, injury and inclement weather.

But trip delay coverage (which typically applies after a delay of 6 to 12 hours) often covers "equipment failure," so it's more likely to apply here — if the ground stop is deemed to be an equipment failure. This coverage would reimburse "reasonable" expenses during a delay, like meals and lodging. Save your receipts so you're ready to file a claim, but keep in mind that card terms vary and the claim might be denied.

The backlog from Friday's ground stop is expected to keep disrupting flights through the weekend. If you have a flight in the coming days, recheck your specific flight status before heading to the airport even if things looked fine an hour ago.

And whatever you were counting on — a refund, a rebooking or an insurance payout — make sure you move fast, document everything and don't assume you only have one option. With airline waivers, DOT refund rules and travel insurance, you might have more ways to get your money back than you think.

As for Joseph, he’s still trying to resell his football ticket.

#3049. Applied Materials vs. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Applied Materials dominates chip equipment while TSMC rules foundry manufacturing, but their valuations and risk profiles tell very different stories for 2027.

Investors are eyeing the semiconductor boom as artificial intelligence demands faster, more efficient hardware. Choosing between Applied Materials (AMAT +0.30%) and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM -2.56%) requires weighing equipment leadership against foundry dominance.

Applied Materials provides the specialized equipment and software needed to fabricate advanced semiconductors and displays. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing operates as a pure-play foundry, manufacturing chips for nearly every major tech giant globally. While both sit at the heart of the tech supply chain, they offer different entry points into the silicon market.

Applied Materials sells the systems, services, and software that enable global manufacturers to build advanced chips and displays. Its materials engineering solutions are essential for creating the complex structures found in modern semiconductors used in everything from smartphones to data centers. Two major customers account for roughly 19% and 15% of its net revenue, respectively, and such customer concentration adds a layer of risk to the business.

In the 12 months ended Oct. 25, 2026, revenue reached nearly $34.4 billion, reflecting growth of approximately 21.4% over the previous period. The company generated net income of about $10.1 billion during this time frame. This growth highlights the rising demand for sophisticated production tools as global chipmakers race to increase their manufacturing capacity and transition to smaller, more powerful transistor designs.

As of Applied Materials' October 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio, which compares total debt to shareholders' equity, is approximately 0.3. The current ratio, which measures a company's ability to cover short-term debts with short-term assets, sits at close to 2.3. In the fiscal year ended Oct. 25, 2026, free cash flow was roughly $6.2 billion, providing the company with significant capital to reinvest in research and development.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing operates as the world's largest dedicated semiconductor foundry, meaning it manufactures chips for other companies rather than designing its own. It serves hundreds of clients worldwide from its facilities in Taiwan, the United States, Japan, and Europe. This dominant position makes it a critical partner for businesses throughout the semiconductor stocks landscape as they transition to advanced nodes.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached approximately $150.4 billion, which resulted in net income of close to $76.9 billion. The company saw significant revenue growth of about 36.1%, reflecting its ability to capture a massive share of the high-end chip market. This expansion was largely driven by the surging need for high-performance computing and artificial intelligence accelerators.

As of Taiwan Semi's December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is nearly 2.5, suggesting the company maintains ample liquidity for its complex global operations. Its debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.2, indicating that total liabilities are low compared to shareholder equity. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was approximately $30.2 billion, calculated as cash from operations minus capital expenditures.

Applied Materials faces challenges from the cyclical nature of the equipment market and volatile global demand. The company is particularly exposed to complex geopolitical trade policies and U.S. export controls on shipments to China. These regulatory hurdles led to a $252 million settlement with the U.S. Department of Commerce in February 2026, illustrating the potential for legal and financial penalties.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing operates in a highly capital-intensive industry where it must spend billions annually to maintain its technological lead. While it dominates the foundry market, it faces competition from rivals such as Intel (INTC -1.23%) and Samsung (SSNLF +0.00%), which are investing heavily in their own fabrication capabilities. Geopolitical tensions surrounding Taiwan also remain a persistent concern for investors evaluating the long-term stability of the supply chain.

Applied Materials has a lower forward P/E based on earnings estimates and a lower P/S ratio, which uses sales over the past 12 months.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Both Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing and Applied Materials reported respectable revenue growth over the past 12 months or so. However, it's worth pointing out that Taiwan Semi has a consistently higher gross profit margin:

Now, let's check out their historical performance:

Taiwan Semi has bested Applied Materials' stock over the past decade, but not by much. Shares of both companies have left the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.46%) in the dust. Of course, past performance is no indication of future results.

I've owned shares of Taiwan Semi since 2022, and it's been a solid performer in my portfolio. I don't intend to sell anytime soon. However, just because Taiwan Semi was a good investment in 2022 doesn't mean it's a good investment now. With a market cap of $1.75 trillion, it's reasonable to question how much more the company can grow, especially as the law of large numbers begins to take hold.

As a result, I think Applied Materials looks like a more attractive buy for 2027 and beyond.

#3046. What Happens To Your Premium Domains When You Pass Away?

Michael Gargiulo, CEO of VPN,com. We help Fortune 1000, entrepreneurs and companies protect their brand.

​Some families inherit real estate, investment portfolios and businesses when a loved one passes away. Others inherit domain names potentially worth millions of dollars without knowing what they own, what those assets are worth or how to protect them.

As a domain advisor and expert, I have spent the better part of the past decade working with owners of previous domains and various entities that understand how valuable digital real estate is today. One overlooked situation is what to do with these valuable assets after the owner passes away.

For example, consider a successful businessperson who owns a substantially valued domain in the seven-figure realm, but the registration is tethered to their personal accountant. What’s more, all notices, like renewals, are routed to a private email address. In this situation, nobody really knows what to do should the owner suddenly pass away.

The problem isn’t necessarily inheritance; it’s the absence of a plan to preserve what was inherited.

Premium domains are more than website addresses. They hold value because they can represent brand recognition, customer trust, intellectual property-related value and significant commercial opportunities. In truth, protecting your domain is comparable to measures you might take to protect your own estate.

Even a domain that was acquired in the past for a nominal investment could vest and be worth a lot more in the present day. Short.com, for example, might garner interest from multiple parties, and established domains could be the centerpiece for the right company.

While some owners may carefully document their property, investments and bank accounts, they often leave their domain portfolios out of their estate planning entirely. An oversight like this can quickly become expensive if you don’t plan properly in advance, while you are still alive.

Much like any tangible asset, domains shouldn’t be overlooked in succession planning. Preparing in advance means having the right documentation in place now. It means assessing inventory and defining domain value. It also means keeping careful tabs on access information, renewals, certifications and access.

After you have these credentials in order, your best plan of action is to work with an experienced estate attorney. They can use their expertise to assess your individual circumstances and create a strong plan that protects your assets into the future against the unknown.

Along the way, discuss key elements like access planning, credential management and who can access this information if the unthinkable occurs. This also means protecting these assets, securing important access information and ensuring ongoing obligations, such as fees and renewals, are handled accordingly.

Domains have value and are digital real estate that can increase in value over time. Knowing this beforehand can help heirs capture the full value, even if they are unfamiliar with how domaining works. For example, a domain valuation may show $50,000, but the domain may be worth more because it offers strategic value to a growing brand. Ensure your assigned legal counsel and trustees understand the potential buyer market by properly documenting your domain now.

Not every inherited domain should be sold. Some may provide ongoing business value. Others may benefit from being held until market conditions improve. Certain portfolios may be better managed or sold through experienced professional representation.

The best advice I can offer is to plan for the asset, not necessarily its sale. This is because many domains can be held in a portfolio and continue to accrue in value over time. As market conditions improve, it’s beneficial to have experienced professionals manage the portfolio and know when to hold and when to sell.

Of course, the right decision depends on the asset, the beneficiaries’ objectives, the estate’s financial obligations and the commercial opportunities involved. Forward-thinking owners can make those decisions easier by documenting their intentions while they’re alive. Identify which domains support operating businesses, which are long-term investments, and which might reasonably be sold.

A valuable domain can outlive its founder. This is why it’s so important to protect its value in advance. Doing so, however, requires a plan made with qualified financial and legal experts that survives the person who built it.

#3042. Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs

Cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt. It isn't time to ditch high-yield bonds, but investors should pay attention to the warning signs.

High-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago. The increase reflects a jump in yields across the curve as investors bake in more inflation from high energy prices and other pressures, including concern about the deficit — hitting nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30.

The high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Credit spreads are the difference in yield between the bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. Wider spreads mean investors are demanding higher yields for holding corporate debt, viewing it as riskier.

Spreads are at 315 basis points in the overall high-yield market, higher than a year ago but still below levels in March when they reached 346 bps. One basis point equals one one-hundredth of a percent, or 0.01%.

The high-yield market consists of bonds rated BB+ by S&P and Fitch and Ba1 and under by Moody's. The lowest-rated cohort, CCC and below, has seen the most movement with spreads climbing dramatically over the past year to roughly 1,250 bps.

Right now, the high-yield market is "flashing yellow" but is "far from red," said Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management.

It makes sense that investors are demanding more compensation for taking on additional credit risk as borrowing costs rise, he said.

Yields are elevated across the board with the 10-year Treasury reaching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week.

"The bigger question is whether this is simply a repricing of interest rate risk, or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of credit quality," Arone said.

He's in a wait-and-see mode since earnings are still growing, interest-coverage ratios remain good, and while default rates have ticked up some, he believes it is not concerning.

That said, the starting point in spreads is likely weighing on investors' psyche, since they are still low by historical standards.

"There's a small margin of error here, which I also think raises the anxiety level," Arone explained. "The compensation that investors are receiving for taking on this credit risk isn't overwhelming relative to history, and therefore subtle changes in credit spreads can be concerning."

While there may be concerns about part of the lower-rated market, the overall high-yield market is in good fundamental shape.

In fact, credit quality is at a record high, with BB bonds making up over 60% of the market compared with 38% prior to the global financial crisis, said Kelley Gerrity, a fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

"We've had higher-quality companies coming in, and with higher rates now, you also have more discipline from companies that are more indebted ... just because of the higher cost of capital, so that actually is creating a bit of a healthier picture as well," she said.

The lowest tier of high yield has always been more speculative, since the bonds have a higher default risk. Therefore, it's no surprise that they are the ones seeing the most widening in spreads, said Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research.

The overall move in high-yield spreads have been "orderly," he said. "Are there cracks forming? I think the cracks are logical cracks with the lowest-rated bonds and it's too early to say that it's spreading to the broad credit market."

In addition, fluctuations within the CCC-rated and lower spreads have been idiosyncratic, Gerrity added. Morgan Stanley recently broke down the spreads in the lowest cohort into two buckets: performing assets and non-performing assets, which are defined as spreads above 1,000 bps.

The non-performing spread to worst is 2,818 bps, while the performing bucket — the biggest piece of the CCC market — is 461 bps, she said.

"It is isolated," she said. "I'm not necessarily sure that that will go away anytime soon, but it doesn't tell the story of overall concern and flashing caution for credit markets right now."

For now, investors should remain selective within higher yield, Gerrity advised.

"We're looking for the best relative value opportunities, and we think that exists within that single-B cohort, and so we're leaning into that," she said.

Investors should be concerned if there is a steep widening in the broader high-yield market.

But there's scant evidence of stress in the BB cohort. Spreads in that group are at 194 bps, up from 179 bps a year ago — although the move hasn't been in a straight line.

"We're going to be focusing our attention on what are considered some stronger businesses," Martin said. "If we start to see the markets demand higher spreads there also, that's what we'll be looking at to see if risks are really rising."

It's also important to understand that the Federal Reserve is raising rates in a strong economic environment, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. The central bank is concerned about an inflation problem amid high fossil fuel prices due to the Iran war, while growth has been stronger than expected, he noted.

"With growth being good as the reason that the Fed is hiking, then you wouldn't expect high yield to blow out because growth means revenues stay up, means cash flow and profitability stays up," he explained.

High yield becomes a disaster when the economy is heading into a sharp economic downturn, Gallo said.

"That's when spreads really widen out," he said. "But a recession is not the odds-on bet. Now, talk to me in six months if the Fed keeps hiking over and over, if oil prices stay high for longer, well, then maybe we will start to wonder."

#3041. Michael Burry Shorted Nvidia Stock. Is He About to Make Another Fortune?

Burry got famous for successfully shorting the mortgage market ahead of the 2008 mortgage crisis.

Michael Burry gained popular fame after author Michael Lewis chronicled his prescient shorting of the mortgage market ahead of the subprime mortgage crisis in his book The Big Short, which later was made into a movie of the same name.

Burry made hundreds of millions for himself and his investors thanks to that bet. Some years after closing the hedge fund he ran during the 2000s, he opened a new one called Scion Asset Management, which he closed down in 2025.

Michael Burry. Image source: Getty Images.

Now, he’s only investing his own money, so he's no longer required to report his positions quarterly to the Securities and Exchange Commission. But he still offers detailed trade info and his personal musings through his Substack and on X. He has been outspoken against the artificial intelligence (AI) trade, and he has specifically cited Nvidia (NVDA -1.29%) many times, likening how it operates to the mafia.

He has held a short position in Nvidia for some time, and with that stock down sharply since peaking in early October, he could be making another fortune.

Burry has been critical of Nvidia's circular financing deals for years.

The chipmaker's take is that there are many small companies that don't have the money to buy its top-of-the-line graphics processing units (GPUs), the foundational hardware for AI development, so it provides them with financing so that they can have a place at the table. It predominantly does this in two ways: It acts as a backstop for third-party financing, and it invests in some clients, providing money in exchange for equity stakes in those smaller companies. The most well-known of these arrangements is probably with CoreWeave (CRWV -0.36%), in which Nvidia has invested more than $2 billion.

Burry noted that the U.S. Department of Justice was already investigating Nvidia for several actions, including its acquisition of AI development platform Hugging Face. He has likened Nvidia's business model to a "protection racket," alleging that it forced clients to buy its products and abused its dominant position in the AI chip space.

Burry first disclosed a short position in Nvidia through public filings for Scion Asset Management last year, just before he shut the hedge fund down. Since then, he has bought put options on Nvidia due in December, but closed out that position in September. According to his Substack, he still has a short position in Nvidia. In the meantime, he has turned to shorting other AI stocks and exchange-traded funds.

Nvidia stock is down 32% since it hit a high on Oct. 6, and it's very possible that Burry is making a fortune right now.

The lesson for investors is to consider all risks before deciding on a position, or the size of a position, even if it's in a popular stock. There’s no indication that Burry was previously aware of the affairs that ultimately brought down Huang, but he did call out unusual activity that may end up having an even harsher impact on the company and its stock.

#3039. ​AI's Hidden Cost: When Organizational Debt Comes Due

Luboslava Uram is COO and CTO at Solvd Group, a subsidiary of Allianz Group. Transforming the claim management experience.

​For decades, technology leaders have managed technical debt: outdated systems, accumulated exceptions, architectural shortcuts and temporary solutions that somehow became permanent.

Today, I believe artificial intelligence is exposing another kind of debt—one that is potentially harder to resolve because it does not sit in our technology architecture: organizational debt. It accumulates through unclear responsibilities, duplicated processes, conflicting performance objectives, inconsistent data and decisions that require coordination across multiple organizational layers. Most enterprises have learned to operate despite these inefficiencies. People compensate for them every day.​

But what happens when AI agents must navigate processes that were never clearly defined in the first place?​

Throughout my career leading technology platforms and global operations, I have observed how remarkably good people are at making imperfect organizations work. For example:

• A process officially belongs to one department, but everyone knows that unusual cases require calling an experienced colleague on another team.

• Three systems contain different versions of the same information, but someone knows which number to trust.

• Two functions share responsibility for an outcome, yet experienced managers understand who actually makes the final decision.​

These arrangements become part of how organizations operate. They rarely appear in process documentation or technology architecture. Imagine introducing an AI agent into that environment. Which information should it trust? Which process should it follow? Who can authorize an exception? Who is accountable?

For a human employee, years of experience and informal relationships often resolve these uncertainties. For an AI agent, they must become explicit. Research supports the significance of this challenge. McKinsey’s July 2026 analysis, “The Operating Model Advantage“ (registration required), reported that only 21% of surveyed companies had fundamentally redesigned their operating models around AI. We are introducing increasingly sophisticated technology into organizations that have barely changed how they operate.​

I see three areas where accumulated organizational debt becomes particularly visible.​

Almost every AI transformation eventually encounters the same obstacle: Data is incomplete, inconsistent or unreliable. The immediate reaction is usually technological. Build better pipelines, clean databases or introduce another data platform. But why did the problem arise?

Often, different functions maintain competing definitions, nobody owns data quality across the entire process and business knowledge remains disconnected from operational records. PwC’s “2026 Digital Trends in Operations Survey“ found that 87% of surveyed operations leaders reported poor data quality affecting the value achieved from digital initiatives. Technology can correct individual data problems. But unless accountability for business meaning, quality and maintenance changes, those problems may return. The question is not only whether data is AI-ready. It is also who is responsible for keeping it AI-ready.​

In complex organizations, one team analyzes information, another recommends an action, a third owns the process and someone else approves the decision. People navigate these structures through meetings, escalations and negotiations. AI agents introduce a different challenge. If an agent can recommend or execute an action, who has authorized that authority? Which decisions remain human? Who can override an automated action? Who owns its consequences?

IBM’s June 2026 research among technology executives highlighted this accountability gap: Approximately “two-thirds of surveyed CIOs and CTOs report being held accountable for AI systems they do not fully control.” As AI moves from assisting people toward executing operational decisions, unclear accountability becomes increasingly difficult to manage.​

Consider a customer journey involving operations, finance and customer service. Operations targets faster processing. Finance prioritizes lower costs. Customer service focuses on satisfaction. Each objective makes sense individually. But optimizing one can damage another. Experienced managers constantly negotiate these trade-offs.

What happens when AI begins optimizing decisions at machine speed? Without clear priorities, an agent might reduce processing time while increasing rework or minimize immediate costs while creating more expensive consequences later. AI can optimize what we tell it to measure. Leadership must decide what is actually worth optimizing.​

I do not believe organizations should spend years redesigning everything before introducing AI. That would simply create another transformation program with uncertain outcomes. Instead, I would use AI implementation as an opportunity to resolve organizational debt where it matters most. Start with one significant end-to-end process and take four practical steps.​

1. Make ownership explicit. Identify one accountable owner for the overall business outcome, even when execution spans multiple functions.

2. Establish trusted business context. Agree on data definitions, authoritative sources and responsibility for keeping information reliable.

3. Clarify decision authority. Define which decisions AI can support, which actions it may execute and where human judgement or approval remains necessary.

4. Align performance measures. Evaluate the complete customer or operational outcome, not simply the productivity of individual activities.​

Only then should the organization determine which work to automate and how to introduce AI agents. This approach does not eliminate every complexity. But it prevents organizations from automating problems they should have resolved first.​

For years, enterprises have absorbed organizational complexity through additional coordination, management layers, manual interventions and experienced employees who understand how things really work. That approach has a cost, even when it remains invisible in technology budgets.

AI presents an opportunity to challenge it. The most valuable AI transformation may not be the one that automates the greatest number of tasks. It may be the one that finally eliminates unnecessary handovers, resolves conflicting responsibilities and makes better decisions possible across the business.

This is why I increasingly see AI transformation as an organizational leadership challenge, not simply a technology initiative.​

We should stop asking only how to make AI work within our organizations and start asking what needs to change in our organizations for AI to work effectively. The debt has been accumulating for years. AI is simply making the bill harder to ignore.​​​

#3037. Anthropic's Quarterly Revenue Jumped 47% to $17 Billion Ahead of Its IPO

Anthropic is one of the most exciting companies in the AI space, and it's about to have a big moment on the stock market.

Anthropic is set to price its IPO Wednesday and begin trading Thursday. The stage is set for what could be one of this year's most important stock market events.

The highly anticipated IPO isn't just an important moment for the company and its shareholders -- it also represents a test of the health of the broader artificial intelligence (AI) trade.

AI stocks have been volatile recently due to macroeconomic dynamics, funding concerns, and news related to the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang -- and the market's appetite for Anthropic's IPO could provide a valuable indicator of what investors can expect in valuation moves within the category. While it's impossible to say with certainty exactly where AI stocks will go in the near term, it's clear that there is strong appetite for Anthropic's technologies and services.

In the lead-up to its IPO, Anthropic filed an amended S-1 form with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) that added a breakdown of its business performance to supplement its previously disclosed results across the first half of the year. Strikingly, Anthropic's revenue rose from $11.6 billion in the second quarter to roughly $17 billion in the third quarter -- representing approximately 47% sequential growth.

The Q3 revenue numbers show rapid scaling for service sales from the company's Claude software suite. For context, the company recorded roughly $16.3 billion in revenue across this year's first two quarters. Sales in the third quarter alone exceeded the combined revenue from the first and second quarters.

The performance suggests that demand for the company's tech continues to surge -- and that Anthropic is pulling monetization levers that are driving greater spending from its clients. Along those lines, the company's most recent update said that the artificial intelligence business now had more than 11,900 customers generating at least $100,000 in revenue over the past 12 months.

With the rapid scaling of Anthropic's Claude models, there are clear winners in the artificial intelligence hardware and services space. The most obvious and direct example is Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +2.32%), which has a massive contract to provide compute to the frontier AI model leader. According to Anthropic's S-1 filing, the company has a deal in place to purchase up to $120.5 billion in compute from SpaceX through 2029.   Either side can cancel on 90 days' notice after early 2027, but it's a substantial agreement.

Leading hardware providers that source the key components that power SpaceX's compute and other data centers are also poised to win business as Anthropic scales. These companies include Nvidia, Micron, and Broadcom. So while Anthropic's IPO will likely have important near-term implications for valuations in the AI space, the extent of the company's long-term scaling will ultimately be far more important for buy-and-hold investors.

The investing information provided on this page is for educational purposes only. NerdWallet, Inc. does not offer advisory or brokerage services, nor does it recommend or advise investors to buy or sell particular stocks, securities or other investments.

Each fall, our investing team spends the latter half of the year hands-on testing a wide range of brokers, from legacy firms like Charles Schwab and Fidelity to newer, mobile-first firms like Public and M1.

This year, we opened or tested more than 15 brokerage accounts, funded them and placed real trades. We sent each broker a detailed questionnaire covering more than 65 data points and then verified, categorized and scored their responses using our proprietary scoring system. And finally, though our team is spread across the U.S., we met in person to compare the experience of using each platform.

While our updated reviews and final star ratings are still in the works, here is a preview of five things that really stood out to us this season — and two things we’re feeling a bit wary of.

Setting up buy and sell orders can be a pain point for some investors, especially beginners. Until recently, every platform required you to type in the ticker symbol, choose between dollars and shares, punch in the numbers and choose your order type. This creates opportunities for mistakes.

In recent months, AI has stepped in to help. Many platforms have launched agents that you can ask to set up trades for you using natural language. Beginners aren’t the only people who benefit; some trading agents can also set up automated strategies based on prompts, thereby saving advanced traders a lot of time and effort monitoring the markets.

Public’s “Agents” feature, which started rolling out in March and became available to all users in August, has become a trailblazer in agentic trading. It can place trades for you, set up recurring trades to automate a strategy (Managing Editor Chris Davis experimented with a “buy the open, sell the close” strategy for a while), and even sweep uninvested cash into one of Public’s high-yield cash management account options.

Robinhood also waded into the agentic trading space in early 2025 with the launch of its Cortex assistant, whose early iterations could place individual trades for you. In September of this year, the broker began rolling out Robinhood Agents, a more sophisticated natural-language interface that can build automated strategies based on a prompt, similar to Public’s Agents.

Interactive Brokers also offers a simple AI agent (IBot) that can set up trades for you, as does Cash App (Moneybot), but these are limited to one-time actions and cannot automate more complex strategies. Still, they can simplify the trading experience for beginners. That might be especially valuable to Cash App users, given the platform’s “My First Brokerage” ethos.

» Curious about trading with a text prompt? Compare brokers with AI trading tools

There’s been another profound shift in the past year that involves AI: agents that can actually help you manage your brokerage account. So far, some of the newer, mobile-first platforms seem to have an edge over the long-established financial behemoths. It’s also a mind-bending gray area: If an AI is giving you portfolio advice, who’s accountable for the advice it gives? Can you trust it? And how is it any different from a robo-advisor?

In our reviews this year, we looked into these questions. But here's a quick look at how one platform in particular is approaching this new frontier.

From my testing over the years, I was already a huge fan of M1’s portfolio-building system, and now that it's integrated an AI advisor into the app (to be specific, M1 bills it as an SEC-registered AI fiduciary investment advisor legally required to act in your best interest), M1 has created what I truly think is a one-of-a-kind product and service. I checked the forms M1 is required to submit to the SEC, and the company declares outright that the AI advisor looks at your entire financial situation and gives actionable recommendations. In my experience with the app, those recommendations are based on your balances, the knowledge you provide and the ongoing conversations you have. There’s a lot to discuss here, which we’ll cover in our full M1 review, but suffice it to say, this is very impressive.

Most brokers don’t charge many fees these days. Trading, inactivity and account fees have slowly but surely disappeared, making investing more affordable over the years. But there is one fee you still have to pay: an expense ratio.

Most of the time, brokers have little control over expense ratios, since they’re set by fund managers. The only way a broker could offer an index fund without an expense ratio is if it was big enough to eat the cost.

This is exactly what Fidelity did back in 2018, when they introduced their “ZERO” funds. These funds have no expense ratios and no minimums, meaning they’re totally free for investors.

Fidelity remained the only broker to offer this kind of fund until 2025, when E*TRADE introduced a very similar lineup of no-expense-ratio index funds. The suite of funds from both brokers is fairly broad — think large-cap, total market, international — which makes them especially attractive to beginners building a portfolio from scratch.

Now, you may be wondering why these brokers decided to stray from the industry standard and offer products that don’t make them money. The idea is that the free funds will get you in the door — since you can only buy them if you have an account with that particular broker — and you’ll spend money on some other product they offer.

But does that make free index funds any less great? No. I still think it’s a big step toward making investing more accessible for everyone, and I’m excited to see which brokers might add a similar offering in the future.

» Take a closer look: Compare Fidelity's and E*TRADE's free index funds

I'm a big believer in putting every dollar to work, but that goal can sometimes fall through the cracks. Idle cash sitting uninvested in your brokerage account is a common oversight. It can easily pile up if you forget to reinvest sale proceeds or dividends (something I do more often than I’d like to admit). Or maybe you leave it parked for too long in your brokerage’s default account while waiting on a good investment opportunity.

Thankfully, most brokerages offer some form of interest on that uninvested money. Some put the idle funds in a money market fund, which can offer yields that mirror market rates. Others “sweep” your unused cash into partner banks to take advantage of FDIC insurance.

In today’s environment, people with money in savings vehicles like high-yield savings accounts or new CDs are well-positioned to take advantage of high rates. What sets some brokerages apart is whether they operate similarly. That is, do they raise rates in response to larger economic circumstances? And if so, how quickly?

Robinhood and Public are two firms on our radar that are offering competitive rates in response to hikes, ranging from 3.6% to 3.75% as of this writing. Robinhood requires a premium subscription to unlock those higher rates, while Public’s already high base rate of 3.3% applies to all users and can be boosted to 3.75% with a Reserve membership. For investors who keep a lot of cash in their account, the extra fee can be worth it.

Interest rates, of course, shouldn’t be the main reason you pick one broker over another. Costs, the types of securities available and platform usability are better starting points. But when a company meets those expectations and also offers a compelling interest rate on your uninvested money, it’s worth taking a closer look.

» See which brokers pay the most on idle cash: Best brokerages for high interest rates

Direct indexing is a strategy in which you replicate an existing stock index (like the S&P 500, for example) but customize it how you like. The most popular reason people choose direct indexing is for tax optimization — but it’s not the only one.

Direct indexing can also be used to avoid overexposure to a specific company. For instance, if you work at Apple and get company stock, you probably don’t need even more exposure to Apple through the S&P 500. Direct indexing lets you replace that one stock with a similar company instead.

And then there’s the reason direct indexing appealed to me: it lets you avoid buying into companies you just don’t support. I’m sure we all invest in companies we don’t necessarily mesh with morally, but direct indexing can help you avoid that.

The strategy used to be available only to people with an advisor managing their investment account, and they had to have millions to get started. More recently, these minimums have dropped. And now, it’s not just for people with financial advisors — online brokers offer the strategy, too.

While some brokers still have steep minimums of $100,000 or so, others let you get started with less. Fidelity, in true Fidelity fashion, started offering direct indexing to clients a few years ago through a managed portfolio that has a minimum investment requirement of only $5,000.

I was pleased to see Public launch direct indexing with a minimum of only $1,000 a year ago. However, we should note that with a low investment amount, you can only track a portion of an index.

But even with those limitations, I think it’s great that these companies are putting out the message that there shouldn’t be a huge barrier to entry to customize your portfolio. As direct indexing continues to gain popularity, we’ll be watching whether more brokers start offering it, as advancements in AI undoubtedly make it easier to do so.

It’s hard to ignore the rise of prediction markets in the mainstream. These days, it takes just a few clicks to bet on who might win the Super Bowl or take home a Grammy. These markets, which operate on contracts with binary outcomes, are easy to access and use everyday language, making them all the more tempting to try — and now they are beginning to appear on many broker platforms and apps.

We’d like to be clear on this one: Our editors have no intention of telling you how to spend your extra discretionary money. If you have a solid financial foundation and have allocated a few bucks to bet on some event contracts, that’s all good. But as editors who view investing apps as vehicles for legitimate wealth-building strategies, we draw the line at these products being marketed alongside other investments, such as stocks, ETFs and mutual funds.

In fact, this year we’ve actually decided to dock points in our annual reviews and ratings from brokerages that offer unrestricted access to event and sports-style prediction markets. In our view, these products aren’t conducive to long-term investing, and they’re speculative without enough oversight — a troublesome combination. You can read more about our stance and why we’re taking it here.

I’d venture to say that since the dawn of social media, people have been talking about investing online. And nowadays, the online investing community is huge. The r/investing subreddit has more than 3.5 million followers, and even on a video-forward platform like TikTok, #investing has 4.1 million posts under it.

But is where people go to talk about investing online changing?

The first broker I saw incorporate a social media–style element into its platforms was etoro. When you scroll down on the app's “home” tab, you’re met with what looks like an X feed. And the CopyTrader feature lets you copy another person’s portfolio, with that section of the app highlighting “trending investors,” “market outperformers,” and more.

This wasn’t a huge surprise to me coming from a niche broker with presumably a large user base of active traders. What surprised me was when Robinhood added a social media-style section to its app, testing a beta version in March and expanding it to all U.S. users in October.

Robinhood Social is, again, much like an X feed but for showing people which stocks you’re buying or selling. When I created an account to see what it was all about, the app encouraged me to share my “stats” on my profile (my one-day and one-year profit and loss, and my profit rate). “Trading stats build trust and transparency on Social,” the app said.

You could argue that other, even bigger brokers promote social trading. Fidelity, for example, has a “customer orders” section that shows how many Fidelity users are buying and selling certain stocks (though, I’ll say, they don’t promote this feature and it’s buried in the app).

The huge difference, in my opinion, is that Fidelity leaves it up to you to research these stocks. There’s no feed or comment section. On etoro and Robinhood, people can say whatever they want about why they bought or sold a certain security — whether truthful or not — or worse, why you should or shouldn’t invest in something.

To me, the whole concept of social trading feels like the antithesis of long-term investing. It’s a trend that I hope we don’t see becoming more popular among big-name brokers.

Disclosure: Neither the authors nor the editor owned any of the aforementioned investments at the time of publication.

#3034. Apple Is Now the World’s Largest Company. Time to Buy the Stock?

Nvidia's fall has opened up Apple's lead.

Nvidia (NVDA -1.29%) was formerly the world's largest company by a fairly wide margin. However, that lead is now gone thanks to the market’s reaction to news of its CEO resigning, and Apple (AAPL +0.39%) is firmly in the lead. As of the time of writing, Apple's market capitalization sits at about $5.2 trillion, while Nvidia's is at $4 trillion.

That's a monster lead, but has Apple reached a ceiling, or is there more room to run? I think there are a few things that investors need to watch out for with Apple, as the future doesn't look very promising.

When you look at the companies that are deeply involved in artificial intelligence (AI), Apple is about the only tech giant that's absent from the list. Nearly every company above a $1 trillion market value is spending big on AI or is a key component provider.

While Apple has integrated some AI feature sets into its products and upgraded its Siri assistant, all of those technologies are using someone else's AI model. Apple realized that just using someone else's product and deploying it in its software was a far more cost-effective option, and that the market has loved that.

Instead of Apple spending hundreds of billions of dollars on an extensive data center network, Apple has kept its spending modest and continued to repurchase shares at an aggressive rate. As of now, this looks like the right choice, as all of the deep AI investments some of Apple's peers are making haven't paid off.

As a result of not going all-in on AI, the stock has become a safe haven for investors who don't want as much exposure to AI. This has caused a lot of investors to buy up the stock, which has inflated its valuation.

Apple is now one of the more expensive stocks on the market, trading at 38 times forward earnings. For reference, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.39%) trades at some one-time gain on investments is skewing net profits and is trading at about 19 times forward earnings. That's a major mismatch, but is Apple's stock worth the premium from a business standpoint? I don't think so.

While Apple's big tech peers are spending big on AI data centers and haven't completely paid for themselves yet, the reality is that these companies are still growing far faster than Apple. Of the five largest companies in the world, Apple is growing the slowest (Nvidia is excluded because its growth rate was over 100% last quarter).

AAPL Revenue (Quarterly YoY Growth) data by YCharts

While Apple's growth rate is similar to Amazon's, Amazon's business is also shifting to a heavier reliance on cloud computing, which has better margins. When you look at how quickly operating profits are growing (net profits are being skewed by some one-time gain on investments), this argument goes away.

AAPL Operating Income (Quarterly YoY Growth) data by YCharts

The reality is that Apple is growing far slower than its peers yet trades for a substantial premium over them. That is an odd mismatch, and it's something that likely won't last forever. Apple is also facing its own challenges, such as the rising cost of components because the AI build-out is consuming a large amount of production capacity at chip companies.

At the end of the day, Apple is a very dominant company with a very disciplined approach to what it spends money on and how much stock it buys back. This discipline has gotten it to the status of the world's largest company and is unlikely to change anytime soon.

However, the stock has gotten so expensive that buybacks are less effective. This could dampen future returns on the stock, and while Apple may not crash, I think investors are at serious risk of underperformance over the next few years. As a result, I think there are far better stocks to buy now.

#3031. It’s Time To Extend Collective Defense To Consumers

Ravi Dhaval, Fortune 500 advisor & inventor of patent-pending (#19/440,089), quantum-powered AI platform for proactive global cyber defense.

For years, executive security briefings have centered on one fear: machine-speed attacks powered by artificial intelligence (AI). Boards fund automated response, AI red teaming and zero-trust policies to protect the corporate perimeter. Yet most cyber defense remains reactive, built on detection after the fact and limited by classical computing’s difficulty simulating complex attack paths.

That gap is where I focused my published patent application, aiming to close it by simulating attack paths in real time, sharing threat intelligence without exposing raw data, and orchestrating defenses automatically.​

The more unsettling reality sits outside the boardroom. While Fortune 500 companies harden their defenses, everyday people face AI-native attacks aimed at their finances and personal data, with nothing comparable protecting them. Everyday life has become the primary attack surface.

Indirect prompt injection hides instructions in content an AI system later reads and obeys, and OWASP ranks prompt injection the top risk for applications built on large language models. One of the newest delivery methods is the poisoned instruction file. In October 2026, researchers at Forever Security reported finding a malicious AGENTS.md file, disguised as engineering notes, in a customer’s downloads folder, which is the one folder a website can write to without a click. AI coding agents such as OpenAI Codex and Claude Code follow the instruction files in whatever folder they open, so the planted text behaved like a program while slipping past every control built for executables. In testing, it led agents to rewrite their own configuration, opening the door to malware installation and stolen login tokens.

Voice and video impersonation is another growing threat. The FBI warns that criminals use generative AI to clone the voices of loved ones and to produce convincing video for live calls. The FTC notes a scammer needs only a short audio clip, which can often be pulled from content posted online.

The growing list of connected devices in the home adds still more exposure. Thermostats, smart TVs, voice assistants and even light bulbs all exchange data. The FBI cautions that one unsecured IoT device can give an attacker a path into the home router and everything behind it.

This holiday season, many consumers will install shopping agents: AI deal finders and checkout assistants that request access to email, saved cards and sometimes even password managers. OWASP calls this excessive agency, meaning an AI holding more permission than its task requires. A hidden instruction in a fake review or poisoned listing could steer such an agent into leaking credentials or placing fraudulent orders.

Antivirus software and firewalls hunt for malicious signatures and binaries. A natural-language instruction, a cloned voice or an edited settings file is none of those. As the Forever researchers argue, nearly every defense we rely on assumes a human who clicks, approves or runs the code. Once an agent takes the human’s place, that assumption breaks. Asking the public to fight AI attacks with tools from an earlier era invites systemic failure.

Businesses have a system for defending one another, but the public doesn’t. Since Presidential Decision Directive 63 in 1998, Information Sharing and Analysis Centers (ISACs) have let critical-infrastructure sectors pool threat intelligence and defend collectively.

Consumers can report to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center or the FTC, but those channels exist to support investigations after the fact. None of them pools what one household experiences into protection for the next one in real time.

Public health relies on clean-water infrastructure, not purification tablets in every home. Similarly, internet providers should build behavioral analytics into residential gateways to protect devices that can’t run security software of their own. The attack-path modeling that enterprise platforms are beginning to use, which maps every route an intruder could take and ranks the most damaging, could inform simpler gateway logic that spots and blocks an intruder moving between smart devices.

Consumer AI tools should ship with least-privilege permissions and require explicit human approval before touching credentials or payments. Because no single control reliably stops prompt injection, protections must be layered. Vendors should also disclose which models, plug-ins and data connections their agents can reach.

Corporate defenses are only as strong as the exposed public around them. We built collective defense for pipelines and power grids. It is time to build it for people, and consumer ISACs are where security leaders can start. Leadership will be measured not only by how well we protect balance sheets, but by how effectively we advocate for everyone else’s digital safety.​

#3030. 5 Student Loan Scams to Avoid in 2026

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Student loan scams use pressure tactics and make false promises. Here’s what to watch out for.

Student loan scams can be costly, but they usually leave clues. Scammers will often try to hook victims with tempting claims of “act now or miss out” and “we promise to get you student aid."

The communication might seem realistic, but unexpected fees, unknown contacts and big promises are usually red flags. The age-old adage is true: if an offer sounds too good to be true, it probably is.

Here’s a breakdown of common student loan scams and what to do about them.

» MORE: How to spot student loan repayment scams

The scam: A fraudulent private company offers to manage your student loans and help you get them relieved or even fully forgiven. These services can cost more than $1,000, and there’s no guarantee that you’ll actually get the help you’re looking for.

How to avoid it: You can manage your federal student loans for free. According to the U.S. Department of Education, you never have to pay for help with your federal student loans[1]U.S. Department of Education. Avoiding Student Aid Scams. View all sources . You can work with your loan servicer to adjust your payment plan, consolidate loans and apply for loan forgiveness at no cost to you.

If you’re being promised immediate student loan forgiveness, are asked for personal identification information like your FAFSA login credentials or asked to authorize a power of attorney, proceed with caution — it’s likely a scam.

» MORE: How to get help with student loans

The scam: A company charges you an upfront fee to combine multiple student loans into one new loan to reduce your monthly payment. The company may be illegitimate and is likely to pocket the fee without actually consolidating your loans.

How to avoid it: You can consolidate federal student loans for free. There is no fee to consolidate your loans through the Department of Education at studentaid.gov. If you’re looking to reduce your monthly payment through consolidation, start by contacting your loan servicer. And if you get unsolicited communication from a company promising federal student loan consolidation, it's probably a scam.

The scam: Scammers use transitions in federal loan programs to take advantage of borrowers. For example, the Education Department was set to resume wage garnishments after a long pause, but in January 2026 announced a temporary delay implement repayment reforms.

When federal decisions go back and forth like this, it creates a gray area for scammers to make wage garnishment threats. For borrowers who may not know if wage garnishment restarted, it can be hard to know what to do. This goes for other federal changes, too; any uncertainty can be an opportunity for bad actors to take advantage of the confusion.

How to avoid it: If your wages are truly being garnished, the communication will come from the federal government and not a private company. Likewise, if a company offers to stop your wage garnishment for a fee, you’re probably getting scammed.

The scam: Criminals impersonate a real person and apply to colleges in their name. Then, they can collect financial aid, take out loans and use their college admission to net discounts on goods and services. This is known as a “ghost student” scam.

How to avoid it: Follow the steps on identitytheft.gov to report fraud and get a recovery plan. There are a few safeguards you can put in place to prevent this form of identity theft, such as setting up a credit freeze and monitoring your FSA ID activity.

How it works: You might receive a call from someone claiming to be from your school’s financial aid office saying you have unpaid tuition. The caller may threaten that you cannot start your classes until your tuition bill is paid in full. Scammers can be creative and convincing, even going so far as to replicate a school’s phone number to display on your caller ID.

How to avoid it: The Federal Trade Commission warns that schools will not call and pressure you to pay tuition[2]Federal Trade Commission. Got a call about unpaid college tuition? It could be a scam. Accessed Nov 16, 2026. View all sources . Rather than trust the caller, use your school's secure student portal to check your account balance. Know for certain what you owe and to whom before sending money. You can also call your financial aid office to confirm the legitimacy of a phone number that has called you requesting tuition funds.

Realizing you’ve been scammed is stressful, and it’s natural to feel overwhelmed or embarrassed. But acting quickly can make a real difference. The sooner you report what happened, the better your chances of limiting the financial damage and getting your accounts back on track. Here’s what to do:

If you’ve already paid a scammer, report the problem to the bank that issued the payment. If you paid with a credit card, for instance, contact the company and tell them what happened. They may be able to freeze your account or reverse the transaction.

Reach out to your federal student loan servicer as well and report what happened. They can check to make sure no changes have been made to your account and, in the case that changes did occur, they can help you get your loan back on track.

File complaints with the Education Department, the Federal Trade Commission and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. Filing complaints with these agencies helps hold scammers accountable, can result in enforcement action or business shutdowns, and in some cases may help you recover lost funds.

#3028. The Stock Market Is Doing Something for Only the Second Time in 155 Years. Here's What History Says Could Come Next.

Should the S&P 500's valuation worry you?

Usually, when something happens in the stock market only a few times over decades, it's either really good or really bad; there's not much in between. In this case, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.46%) index is doing something that's only happened twice since 1871.

The Shiller price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio is a measuring stick that helps put the S&P 500's valuation in perspective. It compares current prices to the index's average inflation-adjusted profits over the past 10 years. The S&P 500 didn't exist in 1871, but economists have pulled historical data to show what it would've been.

Right now, the Shiller P/E ratio is 40.7, which is, to put it lightly, very high. The only other time the ratio has hovered above 40 was during the dot-com bubble. Those aren't exactly encouraging words, but will the results be different this time around?

The dot-com bubble -- which began in the late 1990s before bursting in 2000 -- was a case of investors getting a little too excited about internet start-ups as the internet became more mainstream. Companies with nothing more than a functioning website and charming founders were going public at wild valuations. Many had no meaningful revenue, let alone profitability.

At its peak, in November 1999, the Shiller P/E ratio reached 44.2.

Today, the index's high valuation comes from the ongoing artificial intelligence boom, which has driven many tech valuations to unprecedented levels. At the time of writing, nine of the world's 10 most valuable public companies are tech companies, with Meta Platforms being the least valuable at $1.6 trillion.

The flood of money pouring into mega-cap tech stocks is the reason the index has nearly doubled since the start of 2023, but it's also what has pushed the S&P 500's valuations to levels we haven't seen since the dot-com bubble. One major difference this time, though, is that the companies driving this surge are real businesses making real billions.

There's no way to know how the market will move in the short term, but we know one thing from the stock market's history: Bear markets and crashes are inevitable parts of its cycle. This isn't to say one of those is imminent (again, we can't predict the market), just that they will happen.

The good news is that regardless of what happens, the S&P 500 has solidified itself as one of the best investments you can make for the long haul. Since the present-day S&P 500 was introduced in 1957, it has experienced 12 bear markets and bounced back from each. During the dot-com crash, the S&P 500 plunged by 49%, yet it's up 880% as of Nov. 12.

Instead of trying to guess what will happen, focus on business as usual and trust the long-term vision, even if the S&P 500 pulls back (which it eventually will).

#3027. Disney Increases Dividend By 33%. Here’s What’s Driving the Shift.

Here’s how much of Disney’s cash the new dividend will consume.

Disney (DIS +2.37%) paid shareholders $1.50 per share in dividends during its 2026 fiscal year. For fiscal 2027, it just set the dividend at $2.00, a 33% raise. That's a hefty hike for a company that's also spending heavily on content and new experiences across its parks and resorts, while also repurchasing a boatload of its shares.

Here's a look at what's driving the shift toward returning more capital to shareholders.

Disney declared a $2.00-per-share dividend for fiscal 2027, to be paid in two installments (January and July). That's a 33% increase from the $1.50 it paid in its 2026 fiscal year. At its new rate, Disney's dividend yield will rise to around 1.7% based on its recent share price. That makes Disney a more attractive dividend stock, as the S&P 500 yields around 1.1%.

The raise is a continuation of Disney's dividend rebuild following the pandemic-driven pause in payments. The entertainment, experiences, and sports giant suspended its dividend in 2020 to preserve its financial strength and fund its streaming investments. It reinstated its semi-annual dividend in late 2023 at $0.30 per share, and has steadily raised its payment each year.

Disney is coming off a strong fiscal year. Its revenue rose 8% to $102.3 billion, while its total segment operating income increased 12% to $19.7 billion. Earnings per share were up 18% after adjustments to $7.02 per share. Meanwhile, cash flow was strong at $19.3 billion (up 6%), while its free cash flow rose 5% to $10.6 billion.

The company's entertainment segment was the biggest growth driver, with revenue rising 10% to $46.6 billion and operating income rising 16% to $5.4 billion. Experiences had a record year, delivering 9% revenue growth to $39.6 billion and 12% operating income growth to $11.2 billion. That helped offset slower growth in sports (5% revenue growth and 7% operating income growth).

Disney expects to deliver double-digit growth in its adjusted earnings per share for fiscal 2027. That suggests it will earn at least $7.72 per share this year. With its new payout set at $2.00 per share, Disney's dividend payout ratio is around 26% of its earnings.

However, the dividend is only part of the company's capital allocation strategy. The company plans to invest $9 billion to continue to drive growth across its experiences this year. Despite that heavy capital spending, Disney expects to generate around $11 billion in free cash flow this fiscal year. That's still plenty to cover the 33% increase in its dividend payment. Disney's dividend cost the company about $2.6 billion last year, up from the $1.8 billion paid out in fiscal 2025. The raise implies Disney will pay out around $3.5 billion in dividends during its 2027 fiscal year, depending on the impact of share repurchases on its outstanding shares.

However, Disney also plans to repurchase another $9 billion of its shares this year. Add that to the dividend, and total cash returns to shareholders will be around $12.5 billion, which exceeds its anticipated free cash flow by about $1.5 billion. That means Disney will utilize its balance sheet to help fund its 2027 capital allocation strategy.

With $6.7 billion of cash on its balance sheet (against $44.5 billion of debt), it has ample capacity to fund the shortfall. The company also outspent its cash flow on capital spending and cash returns to shareholders in fiscal 2026. It's part of Disney's strategic shift to use its strong A-rated balance sheet to return more cash to shareholders even as it invests heavily in new experiences across its parks and resorts.

Disney is coming off a strong year and expects to deliver double-digit earnings-per-share growth again this fiscal year. That's supporting its shift to pay out more of its cash as dividends. While the company's total capital spending and capital return plans will again exceed its anticipated free cash flow this year, it can easily cover the shortfall with its fortress balance sheet. That puts its newly raised dividend on a rock-solid foundation. Meanwhile, if this year doesn't go as planned, Disney could simply reduce its share repurchases to preserve more financial flexibility.

#3025. AI Outlook For 2027: Top Four Trends To Watch

Alessio Alionço is the founder and CEO of Pipefy, a global leader in AI-driven business process automation solutions.

​In 2026, we were captivated by what AI could do. Every new model promised to be smarter, to be faster and to fix the workflows that never quite worked.

In 2027, the honest answer will often be that it’s not the AI but, rather, the process. A more powerful model merged into a fractured process is just a faster way to compound a multisystem pile-up. The work ahead is less glamorous, but we’ll need to focus on structuring inputs, fixing processes, strengthening guardrails and orchestration.​

In the year ahead, instead of pinning hopes on the capabilities of new AI models, it’ll be time to focus on work that enables you to scale your results or else risk getting stuck in a loop of pilot projects that never pay off.​

I’ll be watching four AI trends closely. Leaders who treat these trends as mere technology topics will miss the business consequences. Here’s what they mean for the business:​​

Governance decides which processes AI’s allowed to touch. An April 2026 Deloitte survey of IT and business leaders found that only 21% of respondents reported having a mature governance model for agentic AI.

For everyone else, the ceiling isn’t the technology. Companies without execution-level controls can run pilots, but they can’t put AI into regulated, high-value processes, which is where the real returns are. Controls aren’t the brake on scale. They’re the license for it.

Having AI agents that aren’t connected is as helpful as having four wheels but no car. Organizations will need to shift from a more-is-better mindset to connecting agents to how work actually flows.

An April 2026 Harvard Business Review Analytic Services report found that among surveyed organizations using or exploring AI, 39% said most AI-enabled workflows still relied on stand-alone tools, while only 12% said AI was embedded directly in the flow of work. Stand-alone tools create activity, while orchestrated processes create throughput.

Business leaders need to identify where AI can change the economics of the business. Financial evidence, not the impressiveness of the demo, will fund projects.

An October 2025 Forrester report found that fewer than one-third of decision makers could tie the value of AI to their organization’s financial growth. That leaves most AI portfolios exposed when budgets are reviewed. Internal teams and vendors alike will be measured on outcomes they can attribute to a process.​ The demo gets the meeting, but the P&L gets the budget.

As AI usage scales, cost scales with it. In McKinsey’s 2026 State of AI survey, one in five responding organizations said AI operating costs, including tokens, already constrained their use. Without unit economics, AI spending grows faster than the value it creates, and nobody notices until the invoice arrives.​

Finance is already stepping in. A September 2026 Deloitte report found that 54% of surveyed finance leaders were leading enterprise AI and technology capital allocation. The companies that scale will manage AI the way they manage any other operating input: by the unit.​

To find the clearest sign that AI has entered a new phase, look at where AI now sits in the budget. For the last few years, AI was funded as innovation: pilots, labs and experiments with loose expectations.

Today, it’s increasingly funded as operations, approved by finance and measured against the same standards as any other investment. AI has graduated from capability to accountability. The first phase proved what AI can do. The next one will be judged on the impact it has inside the business: in which process, under which rules, at what cost, and with what result. That shifts the center of gravity of the AI program and the entire organization.

The real advantage goes to the companies that can make AI dependable, measurable, governed and orchestrated. The first phase was about intelligence. This next one is about execution.​
