That is up 25% in the quarter and more than 6x year-over-year.

We originated around BRL 3.5 billion in the quarter alone, and our market share went from 2.4% a year ago to 7.3% in September, and this growth is profitable. The product runs at a marginal ROE above 80%. Payroll clients generate 8.6x the revenue of our average client and 67% of these contracts come with an insurance policy. On risk, we are well diversified across more than 370,000 employers with no meaningful concentration in any single company or sector. First payment defaults averaged around 7.8% in the second quarter, and we monitor every cohort closely month by month. We have now issued 5 million contracts since launch.

Every one of them helps us know the client better and serve them across other products. That is the flywheel we are building. To sum up, consistent execution, a credit book that keeps growing quickly, mostly through secured products and clients we know with disciplined underwriting and strong returns. With that, I will hand it over to Andre Cazotto, who will cover our financial results, asset quality and capital.

Andre Cazotto: Thank you, Danilo. Moving to the next slide. Let me walk you through the evolution of our delinquent metrics and explain the dynamics behind these curves. On the left, early NPL, which are loans between 15 and 90 days past due, it rose to 9.2% from 7.5% in the second quarter. Two things explain this movement. First, portfolio aging, which added 127 basis points, reflecting the natural aging of our portfolio, particularly in private payroll loans. And second, the Desenrola program, which added 118 basis points. The Desenrola effect comes from clients who renegotiated their debt under the program in the second quarter but did not keep up with their new installments.

Because the renegotiated contracts move out of the 90 days plus bucket, these clients now show up again in early NPL. Excluding the Desenrola effect, early NPL would have been 8% in the quarter, and we expect it to come back to 7.9% by the end of the year. This shows the stability of this metric over the last 18 months, which has remained in a range between 7.5% and 8.5% since the third quarter of 2025. NPL over 90 days reached 10.7%, up from 9.8% in the second quarter. The increase in NPL over 90 days is primarily a function of portfolio aging, which added 307 basis points.

As our vintages mature, a larger share of the book naturally migrates into larger stages of delinquency. This is a mechanical expected dynamic for a portfolio that has grown as fast as ours, no sign of deterioration. We expect NPL over 90 days to reach 12.7% by the end of the year. These NPL metrics reflect our current 360-day write-off policy. And in a few slides, I will walk you through the new write-off policy we will implement starting next quarter. Stage 3 formation came in at 4.6% in the third quarter compared to 3.6% in the second quarter. As we explained last quarter, the second quarter figure benefited from the Desenrola renegotiated program.

And excluding that effect, stage 3 formation would have been around 4%. The third quarter level, therefore, reflects the normalization of this one-off benefit, combined with the natural aging of the portfolio and our deliberate strategy of intentional risk taken in private payroll loans, the increase in our Stage 2 portfolio was also partially driven by a higher portion of customers enrolling in the Desenrola program, who had already exceeded our 360-day write-off threshold. As these customers entered the renegotiated program, their previously writing off exposures were restated in our balance sheet, contributing to both Stage 3 formation and the overall Stage 3 outstanding balance.

Importantly, this effect reflects the reactivation of previously written off exposures through renegotiations, rather than a deterioration in the underlying credit quality of our performing portfolio. Now moving to the next slide on coverage. Stage 3 closed the quarter at 71.9% versus 74.1% in the second quarter. The reduction in stage 3 coverage is primarily related to the Desenrola program. Loans renegotiated under the program benefit from an FGO guarantee, the operations guarantee fund covering 50% of the outstanding exposure. This increases expected recovery and lowers the LGD of those loans. So they carry lower provisioning needs and mechanically reduce the overall stage 3 coverage ratio. It's a mix effect not changing provisioning standards or in risk appetite.

Excluding this effect, stage 3 coverage would be 76.4% in the quarter. Moving to financial margin. Net interest income reached BRL 2.2 billion, up 9% quarter-over-quarter and 70% year-over-year. To deep dive into our margin dynamics, we are now also showing our net interest margin with clients which measures the margin generated by the financial products we offer to our clients, excluding the effect of our treasury and cash position. Net interest margin with clients remained stable at 27.3% in the third quarter compared to 27.4% in the previous quarter. Our consolidated net interest margin came in at 18.8% compared to 19.4% in the second quarter.

This movement mainly reflects a larger share of cash in our balance sheet following the market funding transactions we completed during the quarter, including the promissory notes and debt security issuances. These resources earning a lower yield than our credit portfolio, so they temporarily dilute the consolidated margin. As this liquidity is deployed into credit, we expect this effect to normalize. Margin of credit products reached BRL 2.3 billion, growing 9% sequentially and 81% year-over-year.

As a reminder, this metric captures the full economic contribution of our credit operations, including revenues from products directly tied to credit origination such as credit card interchange and credit insurance, while excluding cash remuneration and derivative revenues, providing a more complete view of the true margin generated by our lending activity. Net interest margin from credit products came in at 27.2% compared to 27.8% in the quarter. Equally important, margin from credit products after losses crossed the BRL 1 billion mark for the first time, up 11% quarter-over-quarter and 60% year-over-year. The net interest margin after losses remained broadly stable at 12%.

Moving to the next slide, provisioning continues to scale with the portfolio, while cost of risk remains under control. Credit loss allowance expenses reached BRL 1.3 billion in the quarter, up 8% quarter-over-quarter. Quarterly cost of risk came in at 3.8%, down from 3.9% in the second quarter and below the low end of the 3.9% to 4.1% guidance range we provided at the beginning of the quarter. Total portfolio coverage reached 14.9%, an increase of 100 basis points from 13.9% in the previous quarter and the highest level in the series. Moving to funding on the next slide. Our total funding base grew 15% quarter-over-quarter reaching BRL 43.7 billion in the third quarter, up year-over-year.

At the same time, our cost of funding improved to 95.5% of CDI from 96.2% in the second quarter. An important driver of this improvement is the strong growth in consumer deposits. As we become the primary financial relationship for more of our clients, a larger share of their income and day-to-day balances stays with PicPay. This gives us a growing base of granular stable and lower cost funding supports a structurally more efficient funding cost over time. During the quarter, we also continued to execute our funding diversification strategy, raising approximately through the promissory notes and debt security issuances we completed in July and August.

These transactions were fully swapped into local currency, so we have no FX exposure from them. They add to our creditor fund structures, consumer deposits and third-party platforms. Together, these sources further strengthened our balance sheet and enhanced our capacity to sustain the rapid growth of our credit portfolio in a disciplined and cost-efficient manner. Moving to profitability. Adjusted net income reached BRL 271 million in the third quarter, up 157% year-over-year with an annualized adjusted ROE of 18.5%. The 4% sequential decline is fully explained by the tax effect we anticipated in our last call. In the second quarter, we recognized a tax benefit under Brazil's Lei do Bem, which supports investments in research, development and technological innovation.

This is a recurring benefit for the year but it was recognized only in the second quarter, which positively impacted our results and adjusted ROE in that period. In the third quarter, our effective tax rate normalized in line with what we had guided. At the pretax level, adjusted earnings before taxes grew 33% quarter-over-quarter, which better reflects the underlying momentum of our business. Moving to the next slide. I would like to talk about Kev, which includes its insurance and brokerage businesses and adds new growth streams to the group. Written premiums reached BRL 939 million in the third quarter, up 14% quarter-over-quarter and 62% year-over-year.

Since the closing of the acquisition in August, Kev generated BRL 56.3 million in gross profit, BRL 6.4 million in earnings before taxes and BRL 4.5 million in net income for August and September. It's important to note that this is the first time we are reporting Kev's results under IFRS and these figures still reflect accounting adjustments related to the conversion of Kev's financial statements to this methodology. They are not directly comparable to Kev's historical results under local accounting standards. In addition, Kev's contribution to our consolidated results is affected by the elimination of intercompany transactions between Kev and PicPay, which I will explain in more details on the next slide.

On the next slide, present our consolidated results by entity. PicPay stand-alone generated BRL 367 million in earnings before taxes and Kev added BRL 6 million. On a consolidated basis, earnings before taxes reached BRL 290 million, and adjusted net income reached BRL 223 million. The difference comes from consolidation, elimination adjustments of BRL 83 million at the pretax level or BRL 52 million at the net income level related to intercompany transactions. On a stand-alone basis, PicPay recognizes its credit insurance commissions upfront. At the moment, the loan is originated, while Kev recognizes the related costs and revenues on a deferred basis over the lifetime of the contract.

On consolidation, we eliminate PicPay's upfront revenue, but only the portion of Kev's cost that has already been amortized, which creates a negative effect in the period. It's important to highlight that this is a timing effect, not an economic loss, with no cash impact. The amount eliminated today will be recognized in our consolidated results over the lifetime of the contracts. As the book of contract matures, the amortization of earlier policies will increasingly offset the elimination of new upfront commissions. And this effect will normalize over time.

In addition, now that we manage our insurance operation as a single business from distribution at PicPay to underwriting at Kev, we are evaluating adjustments to the commission structure between the two companies, which could further reduce this effect. On capital side, we closed the quarter with a total capital ratio of 15% and a common equity Tier 1 ratio of 13%. And both including the excess capital held at our holding company in the Netherlands. The sequential reduction mainly reflects the closing of the Kev acquisition in August, which had 180 basis points impact on our capital ratio. Moving to the next slide.

Starting the fourth quarter of 2026, we will refine our write-off policy exclusively for our unsecured personal loans portfolio, reducing the write-off period from 360 to 120 days past due. This change is strictly limited to this portfolio with all other credit products, maintaining their existing 360-day write-off policy. The primary rationale behind this change is to ensure that our reported asset quality metrics, particularly NPL over 90 days better reflect the underlying performance of our credit portfolio by mitigating the impact of portfolio aging on reported indicators. This is particularly relevant for a fast-growing credit platform like PicPay where portfolio growth and aging dynamics can significantly influence reported asset quality trends.

This refinement also brings a write-off policy closer to industry practices, including Nubank, which we consider a relevant benchmark given the similarities in customer profiles and unsecured lending products. Importantly, this is not a response to credit deterioration or changes in market conditions. Our credit portfolio remains healthy with underlying asset quality trends performing in line with our expectations. The change does not affect our underwriting standards, risk appetite, collection strategy or recovery efforts. It's also purely an accounting effect with no impact on our cash position. We will continue pursuing recoveries on written-off loans through our existing collection process. Turning to the financial implications.

We expect the implementation of the new policy in the fourth quarter '26 to result in a onetime negative impact of approximately BRL 325 million on our quarterly earnings. In terms of the asset quality metrics, considering the 120-day write-off policy for unsecured personal loans and the 360-day policy maintaining for all other products, we expect our consolidated NPL over 90 days ratio to reach approximately 6.8% in the fourth quarter of 2026, reflecting the mechanical reduction in older delinquent exposures following the policy change. Looking at the breakdown, NPL over 90 days for our unsecured personal loans portfolio stabilizes earlier and at a slightly lower level than the consolidated ratio.

As the portfolio continues to grow and age, we expect our consolidated NPL over 90 days ratio to progressively normalize at around 9% from the second quarter of 2027 onwards, a level where we expect it to stabilize. This trajectory is mainly driven by the aging of our private payroll loans portfolio, which maintains the 360-day policy. From a capital perspective, we expected an associated of approximately 150 basis points on our regulatory capital ratio. Importantly, this impact is already incorporated into our capital planning and does not change our expectations for credit portfolio growth or capital requirements in 2027.

Looking ahead, even after absorbing the impact of the write-off policy change in the fourth quarter, we expect to close the year with a total capital ratio between 13% and 13.5%. And a common equity Tier 1 ratio between 11% and 11.5%. These levels are comfortably above the regulatory minimum of 8.5%, which already includes the conservation buffer and give us the flexibility to continue our growth trajectory in 2027. In addition, with our adjusted ROE nearing 20% and expect it to keep growing over time we have a tremendous capacity to generate capital organically to support our growth. With that, I will now hand the call back to Eduardo Chedid, who will present our guidance and his final remarks.

Eduardo Simoes: Thank you, Andre, and thank you, Danilo. Let me close with our guidance for the fourth quarter and the full year, and then a final few remarks. As in previous quarters, our guidance is for PicPay on a stand-alone basis, excluding Kev so that it is directly comparable with what we gave you in August. For the fourth quarter, under our current write-off policy, we expect the credit portfolio to reach BRL 37.1 billion, managerial revenues of approximately BRL 4.2 billion, net interest income of BRL 2.25 billion and gross profit of BRL 1.33 billion. Quarterly cost of risk should remain between 3.7% and 3.9%.

On that basis, adjusted earnings before taxes should be around BRL 466 million and adjusted net income, around BRL 334 million. As Andre explained, in the fourth quarter, we will also move our unsecured personal loan book to 120-day write-off. We are therefore showing you the full year on both basis, the current policy and the new one, so that you can see exactly what changes and what does not. What does not change revenues and net interest income. Under either policy, we expect managerial revenues of roughly BRL 15.2 billion for the year and net interest income of BRL 8.1 billion. What changes is the time of provisions.

And here, I want to pause on the first column for a moment. Under the current policy, we expect full year adjusted net income of approximately BRL 1.06 billion, and IFRS net income of approximately BRL 1 billion. For a company that reported its first full year of profit in 2023, crossing BRL 1 billion of net income in a single year is a milestone. It reflects what this business is now capable of generating and that earning power does not change with the accounting policy. Under the new policy, the same year shows approximately BRL 733 million of adjusted net income.

The difference being the onetime charge of approximately BRL 325 million recognized in the fourth quarter that Andre described. The credit portfolio closes the year at BRL 34.6 billion as loans passed 120 days are removed from the balance sheet. Beyond 2026, as Andre noted, we expect NPL over 90 days to stabilize at around 9% in the second half of 2027. Before we open for questions, let me put two items from this call in context. The first is Kev. We are very pleased with this acquisition and more confident in it today than when we signed. The reason is simple. Insurance is one of the most natural products to distribute inside an ecosystem like ours.

We already have 11 million active policies in the PicPay base, growing 39% a year. Kev brings the underwriting, the product capability and a solid pipeline of other distribution partners. It wrote BRL 939 million in premiums this quarter, up 62%. Putting distribution and underwriting in under one roof is what makes this a new engine for the group. As Andre explained, in these first months, the elimination of intercompany commissions reduces our consolidated results. That is a timing effect with no cash impact. as the book of contracts matures, the amortization of earlier policies increasingly offset the elimination of new ones, and we expect this effect to reverse over the course of 2027. The second is the write-off policy.

We're moving our unsecured personal loan book to 120 day write-off because a portfolio that has grown as fast as ours carries aging effects that make our reported NPL harder to read than it should be. The new policy reduces that distortion and it puts our asset quality metrics on the same basis as Nubank's, which we see as the relevant benchmark for this product. I want to be clear that this has nothing to do with any deterioration in asset quality. Cost of risk is at the low end of our range. Underlying trends are in line with our expectations, and we remain confident in our ability to keep expanding the credit portfolio in 2027.

With that in context, here's what I think this quarter tells you about PicPay. It tells you the model scales. Revenue per client up 58% and cost to serve up 20%. Efficiency ratio down 11 points in a year with AI adoption across operations becoming an increasingly important lever. It also tells you the model is diversified. 73% of our revenues comes from sources with lower or no credit risk, which is what allows us to grow credit with discipline. And it tells you the model is predictable, 9 guidance metrics, 9 beats. A full year outlook, we are confident enough to give you under the two accounting policies at once.

And on the underlying basis, our first year with more than BRL 1 billion of net income. Growth with discipline is what we set out to build. This quarter is what that looks like in practice. A larger ecosystem, a more efficient company and a credit business growing in a way we can forecast and explain. Thank you for your time and for your trust. Andre, Danilo and I are now happy to take your questions. Operator, please open the line.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from the line of Gustavo Schroden from Citi.

Gustavo Schroden: Congrats on the solid growth. Now let me explore this move from 360-day to 120-day write-off policy. So my first question here is why now? I think it is important you explain us why are you changing the debt at this moment? And also, we should expect some improvement in reported NPLs numbers as we show it that should go down to around 6%, if I'm not wrong, considering your slides. But it is stabilizing in 2027 onwards. So what are the key assumptions behind that stabilization?

So more specifically, if we look through both the accounting change and the increased contribution from payroll and other secured loans, does management believe the unsecured portfolio has already reached this steady-state loss profile? Or should we still expect further normalization in underlying credit performance over the next few quarters?

Andre Cazotto: Thanks, Gustavo. It's Andre here. Thanks for your question. So starting with the first part of the question, why now? It's because now we have history to support this change. We have a much more mature origination business here at PicPay. So we have more history, we have more data, and we have a book that continues to scale and season for us to see how our portfolio actually is performing over its full time and how well our indicators really represent the quality of the assets.

So at the end of the day, I think that our main goal with this change is to make sure that our reported asset quality metrics, especially the overnight days are reflecting the real underlying performance of our portfolio and not just how old it's getting, right? Because for a fast-growing credit platform like us, it's really important. If you take a look at the older policy under 136 days, the NPLs over 90 days continues to carry balances, there are almost a year past due. So the metric keeps going up as the book is aging, right? Even when the credit is performing in line with our expectations.

So under 360 days, you can see that the line just keeps climbing, right? So the change to 120 days significantly reduces these aging effect on our reported metrics. In terms of the level that we are achieving, first of all, we're going to see that metric going to 6.8% in Q4 and should stabilize at around 9% from the second quarter 2027 onwards. Very important to break down here because the unsecured book will stabilize even earlier at slight lower level than we have in the consolidated number that is 9%. So what is basically driving the consolidated ratio to around 9% is the aging of the private payroll loan, which stays at 360 days policy.

Gustavo Schroden: I see. I see. If I may be still on that, you presented that you were expecting a BRL 325 million one-off impact in the fourth quarter and also an impact in 150 basis points on capital. Could you explain us from or the nature of this impact where this impact is coming from?

Andre Cazotto: All right. So just to be precise here, Gustavo, BRL 325 million is the impact on the net income after taxes in the fourth quarter. So it's a onetime effect. There is no cash effect. It's just an accounting effect here. So basically, the loans that were already largely provisioned and the BRL 325 million is essentially the remaining portfolio. So what we are doing, we're bringing forward the recognition of the losses that under the 360-day policy would be gone through our P&L over the coming quarters anyway. In terms of the capital effect, it's exactly what we said. We're expecting around 150 basis impact because the accounting losses reduces the equity, but that's already in our capital plan.

We still expect to close the year with a total capital ratio between 13% to 13.5%.

Gustavo Schroden: Okay. So just to summarize, you are changing because now you have more data and you have, let's say, a relevant book to change? Are you still comfortable with asset quality metrics to keep growing at the same pace, right?

Andre Cazotto: Correct, Gustavo. And there's also a second point here that is the comparability, right? Because this change in the write-off policy is bringing us much closer to Nubank. That is our main benchmark given that we have a very similar client and product profile. So it becomes much easier to put it side by side.

Mario Pierry: Okay. So basically, then you're saying that this excess capital is going to be moved to the...

Mario Pierry: And just to be clear, this capital is invested is it in dollars today? Or what currency is it?

Eduardo Simoes: Basically, the -- remember that the proceeds of the IPO, so in U.S. dollars that we can bring back to Brazil.

Mario Pierry: Okay. All right. And then my second question is related to Kev, right? Like as you show like a net income of like about $4 million -- BRL 4 million. And then a negative contribution of BRL 52 million for the consolidated, right? So my question is this BRL 5 million on a stand-alone seems a little bit lower than what we were thinking originally. Is this solely because we're talking about IFRS rather than they are GAAP.

Andre Cazotto: That's right, Mario. It's accounting of the business. So remember that we said that we were expecting Kev to contribute in a stand-alone basis between BRL 80 million to BRL 100 million, right? So those numbers that we shared before were under the IFRS 4. That's the framework that SUSEP, the Brazilian insurance regulator works with. And it's how Kev has always reported their IFRS numbers. But now that Kev is fully consolidated into our international, let's say, financial statements, we have to move to the IFRS 17, that is the current IFRS standard for insurance contracts. And basically what our auditors are requiring for the consolidation.

So just to share some additional color for Q4 on Kev contribution in a stand-alone basis under the IFRS 17. We expect Kev's stand-alone net income for the fourth quarter to be between BRL 35 million to BRL 45 million, before the consolidation adjustments. And the biggest difference that we have between the IFRS 4 and the IFRS 17 is that basically under the IFRS 4, a good part of the, let's say, revenue recognition of the policies shows up early. And on the IFRS 17, we can say that the profit on each contract, it's basically gradually released over the life of the coverage.

So these are the main changes between both methodologies, but it's just an accounting not a business. If you take a look at the total profit over the life of the contracts will not change, and there is no impact on cash or the economics of the business. But just to reiterate, considering these IFRS 17, we believe that Kev on a standalone basis and before the consolidation adjustments should contribute to something around BRL 35 million and BRL 45 million.

Mario Pierry: Okay, clear. And then on the guidance that you gave for the fourth quarter, on Page 28, right, the IFRS net income of BRL 327 million. This is excluding Kev.

Mario Pierry: Should we assume another negative impact of around BRL 50 million?

Andre Cazotto: Early to say it's going to be exactly the same BRL 50 million, but should have some negative contribution. And basically, what happens here, Mario. First of all, we're expecting to normalize that by 2027 onwards. So it's a timing effect. It's not a cash or economic loss. So what happens is that PicPay books the credit insurance commission upfront when the law is originated, and Kev basically recognized all the related cost and revenues over the lifetime of the contract. So when we consolidate both entities, we basically eliminated the PicPay full upfront revenue, but only a very small part of the Kev cost that has already been amortized. So that's what drives a negative effect.

But of course, that has come back into the results over the life of the contracts. So like I said, we're expecting that to normalize. There is a natural, let's say, maturation of the book of contracts over time. So once the amortization of the older policies, we believe that could start offsetting the elimination of new commissions, but also now that we are handling the business -- the insurance business as a single, let's say, business model from distribution on PicPay and the underwriting with that, we can also look and evaluate changes in the commission structure between the two companies. So also that could help us to reduce this negative effect faster.

So we believe that by beginning of 2027, you should expect that to normalize.

Operator: Our next question comes from Dan Dolev from Mizuho Group.

Dan Dolev: Eduardo, really nice results. Congrats. I wanted to ask you a little bit more on the AI efficiencies and the return that you've seen on those really impressive to see that and just wanted to know like how the efficiency gain results and the AI developments are helping PicPay and what else can be done in 2027 on that front?

Eduardo Simoes: Hi, Dan. This is Eduardo. There are many -- I'd say in many dimensions, we can see that happening on a day-to-day basis. And if you look at, let's say, code being shipped. We have a gain of, let's say, same developers are actually shipping around 60% more codes than before. And we also have around 30% of more people actually coding because of that, which in the end of the day, it accounts for more than 100% of productivity gains on coding itself.

Another thing that is quite important is that right now, every third-party contract, especially software contracts that we have and is due in the next months, we go through an analysis, which is can we actually do it ourselves or we want to keep buying. And either of those decisions, they come with a reduction of costs. So we've had some really, let's say, important third-party software that we've been replacing. And you can see already that in the numbers, and you will see it even more in the coming months. So there are plenty of new things happening on the let's say, productivity and cost avoidance part.

Another one is basically -- you know that we've migrated most of our customer service into AI, and it's been going on for quite a while. Basically, we're doing the same thing that we used to do by actually spending 3% of the previous cost, and we've avoided hiring an additional 3,000 customer service representatives in the last two years. And all that also in terms of token consumption, it basically went through the roof. But at the same time, we had a 98%, let's say, cost reduction on the token unit cost per token. So it means that we've been managing really well the cost of using AI as well as gaining all the productivity from it.

And besides that, basically, if you look at the let's say, the top of line and more revenues coming from that. Lots of new initiatives also with our clients. Our PicPay AI assistant, for example, and we're on the second version of it, and it includes many things that we believe that we are basically ahead of most of the -- of our peers. It's multitask. So now you can basically have a, let's say, a complex instruction like, "Hey, I need to pay all of my bills, they're due this week. I still need to keep BRL 5,000 in my wallet balance.

Please let me know which investments should withdraw money from." And then it will perform all of those tasks at once and allow you with one single command to withdraw money from the, let's say, the investments with worst yields pay for your bills as well as end up with a BRL 5,000 balance for the remaining of the month. So this is quite a different set of skills we're introducing on the small and medium businesses. For example, we've launched already an agent for marketing that basically can set up a new campaign for the small and medium businesses.

And actually, it will shoot that campaign for our more than 72 million clients and geo located as well as directly to the, let's say, the most relevant profile of customers. So many things also on the, let's say, customer side of the business. So basically, I'd say those are just a few examples of how it's basically contributing. So the top line as well as to the bottom line of the company.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our next question comes from Matthew Inglis from RBC.

Matthew Inglis: So on the private payroll loans, you have over 80% marginal return on equity with strong revenue per active compared to the broader consumer base or customer base. And you grew market share by, call it, 100 basis points quarter-over-quarter. But as more competitors enter the space, are you seeing or expecting any changes to pricing or underwriting behavior. How sustainable do you think these returns are as that portfolio matures?

Eduardo Simoes: Here. Yes, we've been seeing in the past months new competitors such as actually the Nubank and other players. But that is not a significant change in terms of pricing pressure, I would say. Again, the way we do it, we price the risk. And in our perspective, we do use the, let's say, the centralized distribution platform from the market, but also the majority of the origination comes from our own platform, our own app where there is less pressure.

Matthew Inglis: Understood. And then on the SMB side, you've seen strong merchant account adds. How is the monetization of the newer cohorts progressing, particularly as it relates to acquiring lending and even advertising? And then kind of holistically, when do you -- when does this business maybe become a bigger contributor to the total business?

Eduardo Simoes: We look at it as a -- the overall business, we look at it as a, let's say, horizon 2, which means that it's still not contributing to the bottom line, but it's picking up really well in terms of growth. So first phase, you can already see, which is more clients coming, 126,000 on average per month now. And if you look at the first half of the year, around 85,000, more usage of products. So it means that we're getting more activation as they actually get more of our products, but still cross-selling and the third wave would be credit products coming on also so that it becomes a contributor to the overall results.

I mean I'd say that if you consider the -- let's say, the early stage in which we are, we're pretty happy with the first, let's say, phase, which is attracting more and more clients and getting them to use the product so that we can start to push and cross-sell more products. It's more or less the same playbook we use on the consumer banking now being used on the small to medium businesses.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The question-and-answer session is over. We would like to hand the floor back to Mr. Eduardo Chedid for the company's final remarks.

Eduardo Simoes: Thank you again for joining us. We keep trying to give you the best guidance we can, and delivery on those that we gave you. We did that last quarter. We remain focused on doing that from -- for the next quarter. And we'll be here for additional questions on the next interactions we have with you all. With that, we'll finalize here, and thank you again.

Operator: PicPay's conference is now closed. We thank you for your participation and wish you a nice day.

#2970. Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

#2967. PowerCompute: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Its hardware refresh and HPC tests will determine whether margins hold once capital returns to miners.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 13, 2026, PowerCompute (PWCM +3.12%) announced that it mined 36% more Bitcoin year over year. For long-term investors, lower mining costs and reduced debt levels dictate whether the company can compound capital over time. Three things management said stand out.

PowerCompute cut its energy cost to mine one Bitcoin from about $58,000 to $35,000 through energy sales and site curtailment, which means shutting down miners during peak-price periods. This operational flexibility allowed mining margins to exceed 50% despite lower average cryptocurrency prices.

Management reduced secured debt from $19.4 million to $1.25 million, thereby reducing annual interest expense to $138,000. Settling loan facilities also removed all pledges on the company's 63.8 Bitcoins and restored full control over its digital asset reserve.

The company is testing high-performance computing, or HPC, by listing GPU capacity at its Oklahoma site on Vast.ai. While HPC requires dedicated hardware, management sees it as a way to maximize returns on its 26 megawatts of power capacity.

Mining output is expanding as updated hardware replaces older machines across existing facilities. Owned power infrastructure and low utility rates protect margins, allowing management to focus on capital allocation.

Execution hinges on completing hardware refreshes and maintaining strict cost discipline. Management is focused on directing its power capacity toward the workloads that deliver the highest long-term returns.

#2965. Why Nike Stock Popped Today

Nike has a plan for profit -- and investors love it.

Nike (NKE +2.43%) stock is hopping Tuesday morning, up 2.2% through 10:10 a.m. ET after the shoes and sportswear icon laid out a new five-year strategy -- and a plan to fix a stock that has underperformed the S&P 500 by 50 percentage points over the past year!

Nike calls its plan "Full Stride Ahead," and the goal is to make a giant leap in profitability -- turning around a business that earned just $2.08 per share over the past year, and delivering profits of $3 or even $3.50 per share by 2031.

How will Nike do that? As just described at its 2026 Investor Day, the plan is to invest in athlete endorsements and in bringing new products to market faster, and to cut costs to improve profits.

Nike will focus on five categories of footwear: Running, training, soccer, basketball, and outdoor. Nike expects to get more than 90% of its money from these markets in 2031. Working off a base of $42.8 billion in expected 2027 revenue, the company hopes to add $5 billion in incremental revenue by fiscal 2031. Of this, shoes will contribute an extra $4 billion, and sportswear the remaining $1 billion.

If all goes as planned, that would yield $47.8 billion in 2031 revenue.

That's the good news -- now here's the bad: According to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence, Wall Street analysts expect Nike to generate nearly $51 billion in 2031 revenue. So Nike's plan for a "turnaround" actually appears to fall short of what Wall Street hoped for, sales-wise.

On the plus side, however, Nike was only expected to earn $2.95 per share in 2031. From that perspective, Nike's promise to earn $3, or even $3.50 in 2031, represents more profit than Wall Street was betting on.

I think this, in a nutshell, is the reason Nike stock is up today -- and why, if Nike can deliver, Nike stock might keep on racing ahead.

#2950. Jim Cramer says Costco's hefty special dividend signals ‘more gains ahead’

Costco is rewarding shareholders with a $30-per-share special dividend, and CNBC's Jim Cramer says history suggests that investors should stick around despite the catalyst moving into the rearview mirror.

The warehouse retailer announced its sixth special dividend last week, alongside a $4 billion share repurchase program. Shareholders of record as of Nov. 24 will receive the payout on Dec. 4. The company also pays a regular quarterly dividend of $1.47 that yields just 0.5% annually.

"With all due respect to the buyback program, which represents less than 1% of Costco's $490 billion market cap, it's the special dividend that I'm excited about," the "Mad Money" host said. "The sporadic special dividend is one of the unique privileges of owning Costco shares."

Costco issued its first special dividend in 2012 and has announced five more since then, with payouts arriving roughly every three years over the past decade. Together, those six payments have totaled $74 per share, on top of the company's regular quarterly dividend.

To be sure, given Costco's track record of these periodic extra payouts, some investors may view last week's announcement as a "buy the rumor, sell the news" situation. However, Cramer said in each of the past three instances — 2023, 2020 and 2017 — Costco shares have outperformed the S&P 500 over the next year.

"That's a very good verdict for those who wonder what to do with the stock now that the good news is out," Cramer said. "It says hold on, don't sell. More gains ahead."

There's also compelling math suggesting that investors should look to reinvest those dividends back into Costco's stock.

Cramer looked at investor returns over the past 15 years. A $1,000 investment in Costco's stock in November 2011 would have grown to approximately $13,321 through Friday, reflecting a 1,232% gain. But reinvesting all dividends into additional shares would have increased that investment's value to roughly $18,411, representing a 1,741% total return.

That's more than $5,000 in additional gains from reinvesting dividends rather than collecting the cash. Special dividends played an outsized role, accounting for roughly 64% of the $116 per share Costco paid in total dividends over that period. "That's an incredible case made for reinvesting of dividends," Cramer said.

"The sporadic special dividends have boosted this stock's total shareholder return meaningfully over the past decade-and-a-half, and they help keep you invested in the stock when it has its occasional lulls," he said.

Beyond boosting returns, the prospect of another special dividend gives investors an incentive to hold Costco through periods of weakness. That patience paid off this year, when shares retreated from nearly $1,100 in May into the high $800s before rebounding sharply this fall. The stock is now up 30% for the year.

"Sometimes I think that the stock's too expensive and it might be a good time to take profits," he said. "But then I remind myself that there's a good chance of a special dividend right around the corner, and it's so much easier to stick it out."

#2947. Data center policy dominated the midterms. The 'Virginia of Europe' is the latest battleground

Spain's government is seeking to tighten restrictions on one of Europe's fastest-growing data center booms, as the country's Socialist prime minister prepares to fight an election. Investors like Amazon, Microsoft and Blackstone-backed QTS are on tenterhooks.

The measure, which doesn't need parliamentary approval, could be approved by Pedro Sánchez's cabinet by next week, and is widely expected to pass ahead of the Nov. 29 elections.

It could potentially cost one of Europe's fastest-growing tech regions billions of dollars in investment.

The government first introduced the decree in August, partly in response to concerns over energy demand and prices. After fierce opposition, it put forward a revised version on Oct. 26, but the proposal still includes strict renewable-energy requirements.

"These requirements could pose insurmountable barriers and act as an effective moratorium," S&P said in an October report. The proposed rules would require 80% of electricity used by data centers to come from renewable sources matched hour by hour, with projects potentially losing grid access if they fail to comply.

Projects already in development or awaiting grid connections would also be subject to the rules, with a five-year transition period to comply.

Data center build-out has quickly become a prominent political issue around the world. In the U.S. midterm elections, CBS exit polls found data centers were a major influence for more than half of voters.

In Spain, concerns over the water and energy demands of data centers are increasingly part of the election debate as the country faces mounting pressure to expand its electricity grid to meet the demand.

CBRE estimates that while developers have announced 10.5 GW of data center capacity across Spain and Portugal, only about 4.5 GW is currently considered realistically deliverable because of grid, permitting and infrastructure constraints.

Alberto Nadal, the opposition center-right Popular Party's deputy secretary for the economy, has said a conservative government would repeal the decree. Recent polling shows the Popular Party leading, with several seat projections putting the PP and far-right Vox together above a parliamentary majority.

Aragón, a landlocked region in the country's northeast, governed by the Popular Party, has emerged as one of Europe's fastest-growing digital infrastructure hubs and is at the center of opposition to the draft rules.

The region has attracted investors with fast-track permits, abundant renewable energy and land, and international cable connections. Aragón president, Jorge Azcón, wants to turn it into the "Virginia of Europe," referring to the U.S. state with the world's highest density of data center sites.

Aragón is set to receive more than 60 billion euros ($66 billion) in data center and digital infrastructure investment over the next decade.

But concerns are growing among residents over noise, water use and pressure on the electricity grid.

Pilar Alegría, leader of the Socialist Party in Aragón, told a Nov. 15 rally that the election would be decisive for the region's future and for protecting its natural resources.

She highlighted the Ebro River, which runs through Aragón, and raised concerns about the resources used by data centers in a region vulnerable to drought.

Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, speaking the same day, sought to reassure investors.

"It would be a mistake to squander that advantage through poor planning or regulation that creates uncertainty for investors," Feijóo said.

Eva Valle, Aragón's economy minister, has also called for the decree to be scrapped.

"It is necessary to halt the approval of this decree, which abounds in harmful conditions placed on the sector," she said at an AWS-organized event on Oct. 27, accusing the government of pursuing "a political agenda."

Amazon Web Services and Microsoft have said their investment plans in Aragón remain unchanged, while urging Spain to provide long-term legal certainty and regulatory predictability.

Google has already put a multibillion-euro data center project on hold pending greater regulatory certainty, according to a report in Spanish newspaper El Mundo, which cited anonymous sources. Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC.

SpainDC, which represents the data-center industry in the country, said the decree would give the group's members the most restrictive data center framework in the European Union and could put 80% to 90% of investment at risk.

"We are going to use all the institutional, regulatory and legal avenues at our disposal" to challenge the decree, said SpainDC president Emilio Díaz.

#2937. Top Wall Street analysts like these 3 dividend stocks for consistent income

Democrats' midterm election win has put the artificial intelligence trade in question, as voters clearly expressed opposition to the rapid buildout of data centers. The stock market could remain volatile amid AI trade concerns, macro uncertainties, and geopolitical tensions.

In this scenario, investors can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios to earn steady income. However, the extensive universe of dividend stocks can make selection challenging. Top Wall Street analysts' recommendations can help investors shortlist attractive dividend stocks, as these experts assign ratings after in-depth financial analysis.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Viper Energy (VNOM) is a subsidiary of Diamondback and owns and acquires mineral and royalty interests, primarily in the Permian Basin. The company reported upbeat third-quarter earnings, supported by recent acquisitions and continued development activity from Diamondback and third-party operators. Viper announced a base cash dividend of 50 cents per share for Q3 2026, payable on Nov. 19. Based on the base and variable dividends announced over the past 12 months, VNOM's dividend yield stands at 5.7%.

Following the Q3 results, TD Cowen analyst Aaron Bilkoski reiterated a buy rating on Viper Energy stock with a price target of $61. The analyst noted that the company delivered solid Q3 results, with production, including oil and natural gas liquids, exceeding both TD Cowen and consensus estimates.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that the key update was the announcement of two royalty acquisitions for $809 million in cash, including deferred consideration, and $82 million of newly issued shares.

Given the recently announced base dividend hike, Bilkoski expects Viper to direct incremental free cash flow toward buybacks. While the acquisitions increase leverage, the analyst believes that Viper has enough capacity for opportunistic buybacks.

Bilkoski noted that Viper has historically delivered one of the highest production per share growth profiles in his royalty coverage, but still trades at a notable discount to the royalty peer average and the company's historical FCF yield range. "In our view, its above-average growth warrants a higher valuation," said the analyst.

Bilkoski ranks No. 525 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.80%. See Viper Energy Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

Exxon Mobil (XOM) reported robust Q3 2026 profits, as its U.S. refineries boosted production to capitalize on the high diesel fuel prices sparked by the conflict in the Middle East. The oil and gas giant announced a quarterly dividend of $1.07 per share, payable on Dec. 10, reflecting a 3.9% increase. This marks Exxon's 44th consecutive year of dividend increases. At an annualized dividend of $4.28 per share, XOM offers a yield of 2.53%.

Impressed by the Q3 print, TD Cowen analyst Jason Gabelman reiterated a buy rating on Exxon stock and raised his price target to $193 from $180 to reflect higher downstream earnings, with the expectation of increased mid-cycle margins.

Gabelman noted that the strength in Exxon's refining business continues to offset Middle East-related headwinds. He added that the company increased its ownership in LNG projects, which should reduce its Middle East concentration over time from 75% to 50% and lower the likelihood of diversification-focused mergers and acquisitions. Beyond LNG, Gabelman expects Exxon's growth in the 2030s to come from Guyana, Kashagan, Permian, and possibly Venezuela.

Gabelman noted that Exxon announced a dividend hike of nearly 4% and plans to maintain buybacks at $20 billion for 2027. "The decision to maintain reduces the pro-cyclicality nature of the buyback," said the analyst.

Gabelman ranks No. 347 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 66% of the time, delivering an average return of 16.90%. See Exxon Mobil Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Williams (WMB), which owns and operates energy infrastructure to deliver natural gas, reported strong third-quarter results. The company announced a quarterly dividend of $0.525 per share, or $2.10 per share annualized, payable on Dec. 28. WMB offers a dividend yield of 3.09%.

In reaction to the Q3 2026 results, CIBC analyst Robert Catellier reaffirmed a buy rating on Williams stock with a price target of $82. The analyst noted that Q3 results were essentially in line with expectations and reflected continued strength in execution across WMB's infrastructure portfolio.

Catellier said that Williams' Q3 performance was driven by higher transmission, storage, and power generation revenues, as well as contributions from the Momentum Midstream acquisition.

He noted that Williams maintained its full-year EBITDA guidance of $8.3 billion to $8.5 billion. In fact, results are tracking toward the higher end of the guidance range, backed by contributions from recently completed projects and the Momentum Midstream deal. WMB continues to target long-term EBITDA compound annual growth rate of at least 11% through 2030.

Catellier expects WMB's long-term targets to be supported by incremental transmission and storage opportunities, including Transco's Southeast Supply Enhancement II project and an 84 MMcf/d expansion of the Garden Connector project.

Catellier ranks No. 667 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 66% of the time, delivering an average return of 9.60%. See Williams Technical Analysis on TipRanks.

#2936. Bam Adebayo leaves win over Rockets early with hip injury, Heat don't expect long-term issue

Bam Adebayo left Monday night's game against the Houston Rockets early with an apparent hip injury.

The Miami Heat star did not take the court to start the second half of their 128-110 victory over the Rockets at the Kaseya Center on Monday, and was instead replaced by Andrew Wiggins to open the third quarter. It didn't appear as if anything happened to Adebayo in the first half, but he was not spotted on the bench as play resumed.

Eventually, the Heat said he was questionable to return with right hip tightness. They then ruled him out for good in the fourth quarter. Further specifics of the injury are not yet known.

Adebayo finished the night with just four points and two assists while shooting 1 of 3 from the field. He entered the night averaging 19.5 points and 8.5 rebounds per contest this season.

Heat coach Erik Spoelstra said after the game that the team was being "proactive" in holding Adebayo out, and that he didn't expect it to be a long-term issue, according to the Miami Herald's Anthony Chiang.

"I saw how he was grinding through it in the second quarter," Spoelstra said, via ESPN. "No matter what he says and no matter what anybody says, let's sit him down and evaluate him tomorrow."

While they don't have specifics yet, losing Adebayo for an extended amount of time would undoubtedly make a major impact on the Heat. Despite losing him, the Heat still managed to roll to a convincing win over the Rockets.

Miami led nearly the entire way on Monday night. The Heat carried a 16-point lead into the locker room at halftime and just cruised the rest of the way to secure the 18-point victory. Giannis Antetokounmpo led the way with 20 points, 16 rebounds and 6 assists. Klay Thompson added 17 points after going 5 of 10 from the 3-point line, and Wiggins had 17 points and five rebounds after stepping in for Adebayo in the second half. The Heat have now won five straight, and sit at 8-6 on the season.

Alperen Sengun led the Rockets with 23 points and seven rebounds. Kevin Durant finished with 22 points, and Jabari Smith Jr. had 12 points and 10 rebounds. The loss dropped them to 11-4 on the year.

#2933. U.S. companies from Nvidia to Apple face a growing China dilemma

BEIJING — How does the U.S. stay ahead of China in the artificial intelligence race? Keep advanced chips out of Beijing's reach, or sell weaker versions to keep Chinese companies reliant on American technology?

The consequences for U.S. businesses came into sharper focus after Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO, ahead of U.S. President Donald Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week.

Huang, who resigned last week amid reports he'd had an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence suspects of being a Chinese spy, had argued that keeping U.S. technology available in China could help the U.S. stay ahead in the tech race.

Others want tougher restrictions on chip sales: The Trump administration tightened restrictions on Chinese companies' remote access to advanced U.S. chips on Monday, seeking to prevent them from bypassing export controls by using data centers overseas.

The question facing Nvidia is part of a broader dilemma for U.S. tech companies: how far to remain invested in China as tensions between the two countries put their access to customers and supply chains at risk.

On Sunday, nine countries, including Singapore and the U.K., signed the U.S. State Department's "San Francisco Declaration" to safeguard sensitive technologies.

"Companies operating in China face competing pressures from Washington and Beijing," a client brief from New York-based consulting firm Strategy Risks said following the Nvidia scandal.

"Actions that satisfy one government can create serious problems with the other, putting market access, investments, and corporate reputation at risk," the brief said.

"Executives need to understand and price out these trade-offs before making consequential decisions."

China's economic slowdown and escalating bilateral tensions have made it harder for American businesses there. Few expect Trump and XI to significantly expand on a fragile trade truce achieved last fall.

Huang was among the tech CEOs at the Xi-Trump summits in September and May, but U.S. officials said Trump does not plan to raise the alleged Nvidia spy case during Thursday's meeting. Elon Musk is travelling with the president, who is otherwise not bringing a business delegation as he did in May.

"American tech companies have been diversifying away from China," Kyle Chan, a fellow at The Brookings Institution, told CNBC, but Nvidia and Apple are "in some ways stark outliers against this trend."

Analysts are watching how Apple CEO John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in October, navigates bilateral tensions.

"Ternus may accelerate a process of diversification away from China that Tim Cook started," Chan said. "But it's hard to imagine that China will not play an essential role in Apple's future under Ternus, given the depth and breadth of China's manufacturing supply chains."

Apple still manufactures most of its iPhones in China, and Greater China, which Apple defines as mainland China, Hong Kong and Taiwan, accounts for around 15% of sales.

"The most defensible path is managed decoupling—not the rolling deferrals and hedged announcements that defined Cook's tenure—but a genuine strategic commitment to building a company that can absorb the reductions of China access without losing the ability to manufacture at the cutting edge," Strategy Risks CEO Isaac Stone Fish wrote in American Affairs earlier this year.

China's economic clout, however, also increases the fallout from any retaliation Beijing decides to enact in response to tighter U.S. policy.

Companies, especially U.S. multinationals, pursued the China market after it began re-opening to foreign businesses in the 1980s. Consumer demand boomed, while local factories produced so much they reached 40% of global container exports this summer. The U.S. AI data center buildout relied on China-made parts.

China has amassed control of the supply chain for critical minerals. Beijing has used its grip on rare earths as leverage in trade talks with the U.S. and the EU.

Despite some buildout of the rare earths supply outside China, "it's just not at the scale that the world needs to continue to build products and for industry to continue to evolve," said Cameron Johnson, a Shanghai-based senior partner at business consultancy Tidalwave Solutions.

He cited looming shortages of yttrium, which would limit the production and repair of airplane engines.

"There's just no road map. That's really one of the biggest issues," Johnson said. "Companies have no idea what they're ordering now, whether they will have access to it again."

#2930. 76ers' Jaylen Brown injures head, hamstring in victory over Nets

Philadelphia 76ers forward Jaylen Brown briefly went down with a potential head injury after knocking heads with Brooklyn Nets forward Julius Randle. Though Brown was bleeding, he eventually returned to the game with a bandage on his head, and played a few more minutes of the 76ers' 135-123 win over the Nets.

The collision between Brown and Randle happened in the fourth quarter of Monday's matchup in Brooklyn, with Brown's forehead connecting with Randle's mouth. Both men were bleeding after the incident, though from different parts of the head.

Brown stayed down for a while, rolling onto his back and covering his face with his hands. The entire 76ers bench soon came out to surround him while he was tended to by trainers. Brown then received additional care on the bench, before returning to the game with a bandage on his head.

Brown eventually left again because of tightness in his left hamstring. He said he will have additional testing on both his head and his hamstring on Tuesday.

Randle, meanwhile, got his bloody lip stitched up off the court and returned to the game as well. Randle was called for the foul on the play, but because it wasn't a shooting foul, Brown did not need to attempt free throws.

At the time of the foul, Brown had scored 29 points and picked up 12 rebounds, thanks to a first-half double-double. He finished with 31 points, 13 rebounds and 4 assists in the 12-point victory.

Joel Embiid led both teams with 37 points, while Randle had 33 points for Brooklyn in the loss.

#2927. Analysis: The Fed's chairman sees an AI revolution coming. Now he has to figure out what it means

Artificial intelligence is about to sweep through the economy. The Federal Reserve is bracing for impact.

"We are at a hinge point in the U.S. economy," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said at a conference he convened in San Francisco on Monday. But exactly when and how the economy could turn, and what that means for interest rates and inflation, isn't yet clear.

The meeting of Warsh's AI task force saw the new Fed chairman publicly asking the questions Americans will ultimately expect him to answer. He hinted at a few of his private views on whether white-collar workers could soon face massive job losses, but he largely left the speculation to an array of experts he has assembled to advise the Fed.

With the technology racing ahead, Warsh won't be able to put off giving his own answers much longer. AI lab Anthropic plans to price the shares for its initial public offering on Wednesday and could raise as much as $64 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation. Vast spending from AI firms is prompting the Fed to contemplate raising interest rates in December to slow down the rate of price increases as the tech sector heats up the economy.

Meanwhile Americans are souring on some aspects of the technology. The Nov. 3 midterms saw voters enact an array of state-level measures to slow down construction of the data centers that are essential to powering AI.

Warsh moderated three out of four sessions at Monday's event and was involved in selecting the speakers. Among them was one of the few prominent Democrats who was willing to speak out against that anti-data center trend.

It is "a very troubling sign" that so many anti-data center measures passed in the midterms, Gina Raimondo said. She is a former secretary of Commerce under President Joe Biden and a former governor of Rhode Island.

Stopping AI "would be very bad for America" and for the people who voted for the measures, Raimondo said.

Warsh didn't say whether he shares that view, and how it would translate into monetary policy isn't exactly clear.

The event was an unusual one for the Fed. The central bank employs a small army of Ph.D. economists who can rapidly weigh in on anything affecting the U.S. and global economies. But in keeping with his long-standing critiques of the Fed as insular and outdated, Warsh has chosen to draw expertise from outside the institution to help it figure out how to think about what AI will do to productivity and jobs.

Warsh has assembled a task force on that issue, alongside four others devoted to aspects of Fed policymaking.

The public heard Monday from one of the three official members of the task force: venture capitalist Marc Andreessen. Warsh went to Stanford University with Andreessen's wife, and the two have been longtime friends. Another task force member, Stanford economist Chad Jones, is on leave and working at Anthropic and couldn't speak during the company's blackout period ahead of the IPO. The third, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, didn't attend the event.

Andreessen is hugely optimistic about the promise of AI as a technology, but believes the government won't let Americans experience its full effects. Heavy regulation in areas such as healthcare and education mean technology can't replace people's jobs in those sectors, he said.

"To the extent our economy is a free market economy, then maybe you could see the, let's say, extremely rapid displacement scenarios people are talking about," Andreessen said. "But we've mostly outlawed the kind of job transition that … both the utopians the doomers talk about."

Warsh returned repeatedly to one scenario for the economy that draws on past experience. The so-called China shock unfolded after that country joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 and moved heavily into low-cost manufacturing. Americans saw prices on clothing and furniture drop rapidly, for instance, but at the cost of severe job losses. One widely cited estimate found the U.S. lost a million manufacturing jobs and 2.4 million jobs overall in the years that followed.

Warsh suggested to one of the panelists that the widespread adoption of AI might produce its own version of the China shock, this time focused on service workers.

"I don't want to hold this too tightly," Warsh said. "But if in some ways over the last generation or generation and a half, the China shock, for lack of a better word, lowered prices of goods in the United States, the way that I heard you talking about the philosophy of this new technology is it might do something for services."

In other words, AI could do, say, legal or administrative work more cheaply than a human. That could lower prices but put many people out of a job.

Warsh asked panelists whether "we should expect disinflation over the medium term, from what AI could do to services."

They largely suggested it was possible, which could mean the Fed might eventually want to lower interest rates over the long term.

But at the end of the day, it is Warsh and his fellow Fed members who will need to have conviction on the answer.

There are still many steps between the task force discussion and any kind of change in Fed policy. First, the three task force members will have to assemble their points of view into a report for Warsh sometime in the next few months. Then the Fed itself will need to debate those results and decide whether or how to use them to shape monetary policy.

But with AI growing bigger every day, the Fed may need to make up its mind sooner rather than later.

#2925. Berkshire Hathaway raised its stake in Delta in the third quarter. It also trimmed a key bank holding

Berkshire Hathaway made several moves in the stock market during the third quarter, adding to key positions and trimming others.

The Omaha-based conglomerate, now led by CEO Greg Abel, increased its Delta Air Lines stake by 12%, scooping up 7.13 million shares. The position was worth $5.37 billion at the end of the third quarter.

Abel succeeded legendary investor Warren Buffett, 96, at the start of this year. Buffett continues to control roughly 13% of Berkshire common stock, Reuters said Monday, after the former CEO donated $5.5 billion to nonprofit foundations.

Berkshire boosted its stake in Delta as the Atlanta-based carrier's shares tumbled 11% in the third quarter, hurt by rising jet fuel prices due to the U.S.-Iran war that pressured the entire airline industry. That marked the stock's worst quarterly performance since the first quarter of 2025, when it plunged 28%. Delta last month also cut its full-year earnings forecast, citing a surge in fuel costs.

To be sure, buying that dip has been a winning investment thus far. Delta is up 3.8% so far in the fourth quarter, while the S&P 500 has dropped 3.1%. Shares are also up nearly 15% over the past month.

Berkshire also trimmed its holding in Bank of America by nearly 6%, selling more than $1.6 billion worth of stock.

BofA was under pressure in the third quarter, falling more than 4%, as interest rates surged alongside stubbornly high inflation and expectations of tighter Federal Reserve monetary policy. At one point in September the 30-year Treasury bond yield surged above 5.6% to its highest level since 2002.

Despite the share sale, Bank of America remains a top Berkshire Hathaway holding, with the conglomerate's stake valued at $24.8 billion at the end of the third quarter.

Berkshire also initiated a position in Bending Spoons and nearly doubled its stake in homebuilder Lennar in the latest quarter.

#2919. JD Vance says he'll decide 'sometime next year' about 2028 presidential run

U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Monday he will make a decision next year about whether to run for president in 2028.

"We'll figure it out sometime next year," he told Fox News host Laura Ingraham in an interview that aired Monday evening.

"I'm not an expert in this but my understanding with a presidential campaign is there's a lot of infrastructure that you have to set up, fundraising, all that stuff and so you can't declare a month before the Iowa caucus that you're going to run for president," he said. "So, you know, I haven't made a decision."

Vance has yet to openly declare any ambition to succeed President Donald Trump when his current term ends, but speculation that the vice president has his sights set on the White House has been mounting for some time. In the wake of the GOP's crushing defeat in the U.S. midterm election on Nov. 3, anonymous sources involved in campaigns told Reuters Vance was among the high-profile Republicans who had begun early preparations for a 2028 run.

Candidates typically announce their intentions to run in the election in the spring of 2027, with parties holding nominating conventions to formally select their presidential candidates between July and September.

Polymarket currently slates Vance as the frontrunner to win the Republican presidential nomination for the 2028 election, with the prediction market giving him a 37% chance of becoming the nominee. Kalshi currently gives a 73% chance that Vance will run for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination. Pressed on 2028 in Monday's interview, Vance said: "When I make a decision, I will be all in on whatever that decision is."

Candidates vying for the Republican nomination face the challenge of convincing voters the party can veer away from unpopular Trump-era policies without alienating its MAGA base.

Vance himself has blamed the Iran war for the midterm election outcome.

"I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, "I told you so": you're right, you did tell us so," he said in a lengthy X post as the results were coming in. "Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let's take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country."

In his interview with Fox News on Monday, Vance said the Republicans got "shellacked" in the midterms.

"We have to take messages from that, but the message that we have to take is that the American people want prosperity, they want freedom, they want sovereignty within their own country and they want us to do more of the good things that we've done," he said.

He added that lawmakers needed to double down on "economic nationalism" and bring "prosperity to the homeland" to deal with "economic pain" in the United States.

#2917. Iran escalates threats as third U.S. carrier arrives in Middle East, tanker struck in Hormuz

Iran has ratcheted up threats against U.S. forces and commercial shipping as a third American aircraft carrier arrived in the Gulf, stoking fears of renewed escalation in the nine-month conflict.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy warned shipping companies against using the U.S.-backed southern route through the Strait of Hormuz, describing it as fully closed and a "minefield of fire," according to regional media outlets citing a statement from the force.

Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akrami-Nia, a spokesperson for the Iranian Army, said the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen until "the enemy accepts Iran's conditions."

Separately, CNN reported Monday that new U.S. intelligence indicated Iran was developing plans that could target senior Trump administration officials with a so-called dirty bomb, or a chemical weapon in Washington, D.C. CNBC cannot immediately verify the report.

The intelligence was characterized as an effort by Iran to develop options rather than evidence of an imminent attack, CNN reported. U.S. officials have held several meetings over the past week to consider how to respond to the potential threat.

The heightened security concerns come after Iranian threats prompted Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to relocate to military housing last week.

"We remain vigilant, monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland," a White House spokesperson said in a statement to CNBC.

Oil prices inched lower in Asian trading Tuesday, with international benchmark Brent crude futures dropping 0.7% to $91.8 a barrel and U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures falling 0.7% to $85.1 a barrel.

On Tuesday, the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations said a tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile in the Strait of Hormuz and subsequently caught fire. The agency did not say who was responsible and urged vessels to transit with caution and report suspicious activity.

Separately, the Iranian navy said four oil tankers had struck mines and caught fire in the eastern Strait of Hormuz over the previous 24 hours.

The escalation in Tehran's rhetoric came as the USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived in the Gulf region on Sunday, joining the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington. That added to U.S. firepower near Iran even as President Donald Trump said the war was winding down.

Trump has sent mixed signals regarding the conflict in recent weeks, alternating between declaring it could soon end and warning of renewed large-scale strikes if efforts to reach a deal fail.

After meeting Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani last week, Trump said the war with Iran could end "fairly soon," adding that it "militarily is effectively over."

Tehran said Sunday that it launched six drones at a U.S. air-defense radar at Bahrain's Riffa air base, the second attack Iran claimed against the kingdom in three days. Bahrain's military said it intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks in a call Monday with Bahraini Foreign Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani and reaffirmed Washington's commitment to the security of Bahrain and other Gulf partners.

The conflict began in late February when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran, prompting Tehran to retaliate with strikes on Israel and Gulf states hosting American military bases. Indirect talks between Washington and Tehran through Qatar have since appeared to run into a stalemate as warring powers disagreed over terms to reach a lasting peace deal.

Washington appears unwilling to accept several of Iran's demands to end the war, including lifting the U.S. naval blockade on its southern ports and lifting sanctions, while stressing that Iran cannot possess a nuclear weapon.

Iran is likely to continue escalating attacks on tankers and container ships, along with occasional strikes on U.S. military targets, in an effort to pressure Washington into offering concessions, said Ian Bremmer, president and founder of Eurasia Group. In response, Washington will likely expand its blockade on Iran's maritime and inland trade routes, he said.

"The presumption is that eventually Iran can't handle the economic pressure and will accept better terms," Bremmer said, calling that view a "misread of the Iranian leadership and their capacity to resist."

Over the coming year, Iran is likely to intensify efforts to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, Bremmer said.
